extraction.body: The stunning decision by Nvidia 's board to bring back Jensen Huang as CEO was sealed by a personal promise from President Donald Trump on Sunday that Huang had not broken national security laws, three people familiar with the board's thinking told CNBC. Several other factors also set the stage for Huang's return and accelerated discussions with him over the weekend, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations close to Nvidia's board. A sharp stock price drop after his resignation and questions about the leadership of interim CEO Colette Kress also spurred the board's decision, the people said. "I convinced them," Trump told CNBC's Eamon Javers in a phone interview Monday morning , shortly after Nvidia announced Huang's return. "I made the deal," the president said. "It was a lot easier to convince them yesterday than it was a week and a half ago. Trump said Nvidia's board asked for guarantees that Huang, who resigned less than two weeks ago, was not a threat to national security. "And we gave them assurances, at least with everything we know," the president said. "We believe he's fine. He's absolutely fine." Senior Trump administration officials reached out to the board overnight Friday to inform them that Huang had not violated U.S. national security laws, people familiar with the board's actions said. After the White House outreach, the board contacted Huang, who joined meetings on Saturday and Sunday to discuss his potential return, the people said. Huang's spokesman did not respond to a request for comment when asked about his contact with the board and other events leading up to his return. The Nvidia founder resigned on Nov. 12 after reports that he had an affair with an Nvidia employee and with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based company Megaspeed who is suspected of being a spy for China. A report of an affair with a second Nvidia employee broke right after he quit. Nvidia's board named Kress, the company's chief financial officer, as the interim CEO while it searched for a permanent successor. But within days of Kress taking over, some employees and investors who spoke to CNBC questioned her stewardship, as many of them clamored for Huang's return. Kress' performances at an all-hands company meeting on Wednesday and on Nvidia's earnings call with analysts a day earlier were seen by some investors as uninspiring and underwhelming. As the board faced those concerns amid a stock drop of more than 25% over the past week, Huang was aggressively working the phones with major tech CEOs who wanted to see him return to Nvidia, according to sources close to Huang. In the days after he resigned, Huang spoke with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman , OpenAI President Greg Brockman , and Elon Musk , CEO of SpaceX and Tesla , one of the sources said. Huang wanted his job back, but he was not sure what the return path looked like, the sources said. On Nov. 17, less than a week after quitting, Huang issued a public statement saying he was open to returning as CEO. "I've seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO," he said. "NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company," he added. "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO." On the same day, Nvidia's newly appointed board chair, Harvey Jones, told analysts on the company's earnings call that the board did "not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." Kress, the following day, told company employees at the all-hands meeting, "Let's move forward." Nvidia's public stance against Huang returning came as members of Congress moved ahead with plans to interview him at hearings and as criticism grew over the company's business in Asia. The Department of Justice and the Commerce Department, in an unusual joint public statement on Nov. 17, said they were investigating Megaspeed for possible diversion of advanced Nvidia semiconductor chips to China in violation of U.S. export control law. "Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the U.S. economy," the departments said. But days later, senior Trump administration officials contacted Nvidia's board to tell them that Jensen Huang himself was not a risk, according to the sources. The Department of Commerce added Megaspeed to a trade blacklist later Monday. Trump, during his interview Monday with CNBC, was asked what Attorney General Todd Blanche had told him about potential criminal liability for Huang and the question of whether Nvidia chips had ended up in China in violation of U.S. export laws. "They did a pretty good investigation, and they felt that he, himself, was exonerated," Trump said . Both Trump and Vice President JD Vance became convinced that Huang was a singular figure who is preventing closed-source model AI companies, such as Anthropic, from getting too powerful, according to a person familiar with the matter, who spoke on condition of anonymity to disclose private discussions. The person said Trump and Vance were briefed on the national security elements of the situation and saw no evidence that Huang did anything illegal or untoward in that regard. Trump believes his administration's close working relationship with Huang gives the U.S. its best opportunity to protect national security and prevent cutting-edge AI chips from reaching banned customers, according to the person. Trump said he spoke with Huang on Sunday, after Nvidia had voted unanimously to reinstate him. "I called him up, and I said: 'I ask you to do one thing, Jensen. Work hard,'" Trump said. "He knows what to do and what not to do," Trump said. "But I just said work hard because if you work hard, there's nobody that can capture what you've done. Nobody, nobody close." — CNBC's Kevin Breuninger and Kif Leswing contributed to this article.

The company announced on Monday morning that the board “voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA.” In its statement, the board says that it received input “from senior levels of the United States government” and determined that “Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” Donald Trump responded to the board’s decision in a post on Truth Social, saying Nvidia “made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO… The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. Several other factors also set the stage for Huang's return and accelerated discussions with him over the weekend, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations close to Nvidia's board. A sharp stock price drop after his resignation and questions about the leadership of interim CEO Colette Kress also spurred the board's decision, the people said. "I convinced them," Trump told CNBC's Eamon Javers in a phone interview Monday morning , shortly after Nvidia announced Huang's return. "I made the deal," the president said. "It was a lot easier to convince them yesterday than it was a week and a half ago. Trump said Nvidia's board asked for guarantees that Huang, who resigned less than two weeks ago, was not a threat to national security. "And we gave them assurances, at least with everything we know," the president said. "We believe he's fine. He's absolutely fine." Senior Trump administration officials reached out to the board overnight Friday to inform them that Huang had not violated U.S. national security laws, people familiar with the board's actions said. After the White House outreach, the board contacted Huang, who joined meetings on Saturday and Sunday to discuss his potential return, the people said. Huang's spokesman did not respond to a request for comment when asked about his contact with the board and other events leading up to his return. The Nvidia founder resigned on Nov. 12 after reports that he had an affair with an Nvidia employee and with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based company Megaspeed who is suspected of being a spy for China. A report of an affair with a second Nvidia employee broke right after he quit. Nvidia's board named Kress, the company's chief financial officer, as the interim CEO while it searched for a permanent successor. But within days of Kress taking over, some employees and investors who spoke to CNBC questioned her stewardship, as many of them clamored for Huang's return. Kress' performances at an all-hands company meeting on Wednesday and on Nvidia's earnings call with analysts a day earlier were seen by some investors as uninspiring and underwhelming. As the board faced those concerns amid a stock drop of more than 25% over the past week, Huang was aggressively working the phones with major tech CEOs who wanted to see him return to Nvidia, according to sources close to Huang. In the days after he resigned, Huang spoke with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman , OpenAI President Greg Brockman , and Elon Musk , CEO of SpaceX and Tesla , one of the sources said. Huang wanted his job back, but he was not sure what the return path looked like, the sources said. On Nov. 17, less than a week after quitting, Huang issued a public statement saying he was open to returning as CEO. "I've seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO," he said. "NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company," he added. "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO." On the same day, Nvidia's newly appointed board chair, Harvey Jones, told analysts on the company's earnings call that the board did "not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." Kress, the following day, told company employees at the all-hands meeting, "Let's move forward." Nvidia's public stance against Huang returning came as members of Congress moved ahead with plans to interview him at hearings and as criticism grew over the company's business in Asia. The Department of Justice and the Commerce Department, in an unusual joint public statement on Nov. 17, said they were investigating Megaspeed for possible diversion of advanced Nvidia semiconductor chips to China in violation of U.S. export control law. "Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the U.S. economy," the departments said. But days later, senior Trump administration officials contacted Nvidia's board to tell them that Jensen Huang himself was not a risk, according to the sources. The Department of Commerce added Megaspeed to a trade blacklist later Monday. Trump, during his interview Monday with CNBC, was asked what Attorney General Todd Blanche had told him about potential criminal liability for Huang and the question of whether Nvidia chips had ended up in China in violation of U.S. export laws. "They did a pretty good investigation, and they felt that he, himself, was exonerated," Trump said . The person said Trump and Vance were briefed on the national security elements of the situation and saw no evidence that Huang did anything illegal or untoward in that regard. Trump believes his administration's close working relationship with Huang gives the U.S. its best opportunity to protect national security and prevent cutting-edge AI chips from reaching banned customers, according to the person. Trump said he spoke with Huang on Sunday, after Nvidia had voted unanimously to reinstate him. "I called him up, and I said: 'I ask you to do one thing, Jensen. Work hard,'" Trump said. "He knows what to do and what not to do," Trump said. "But I just said work hard because if you work hard, there's nobody that can capture what you've done. Nobody, nobody close." — CNBC's Kevin Breuninger and Kif Leswing contributed to this article.

extraction.body: Less than two weeks after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after his extramarital affair raised national security concerns, Nvidia's board announced Monday that it had reinstated him as president and chief executive “effective immediately." Nvidia's board of directors voted unanimously to reinstate Huang after a series of discussions and meetings with him, Nvidia said in a statement, noting that the board received input from senior levels of the U.S. government. “Based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” President Trump signaled he strongly supported Huang's reinstatement. In an interview with CNBC, he declared Nvidia had been "exonerated" and on social media said the company had made an “absolutely GREAT decision.” "The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy," Trump said on Truth Social. Trump said the U.S. attorney general had confirmed the government does not possess evidence that Huang engaged in unlawful conduct. He added he had "gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure." The news sent Nvidia stock soaring nearly 30%, regaining most of its losses. But as tech leaders and venture capitalists rejoiced — “The mistake has been corrected,” billionaire tech leader Elon Musk posted on X — prominent lawmakers in Washington, on both sides of the political aisle, expressed skepticism about Huang's reinstatement and called for more congressional oversight. Newt Gingrich, the former Republican speaker of the House, posted on X that there was something "profoundly wrong" with Huang having a relationship with a Chinese spy and helping China get advanced computer chips. "Congress should really dig into this as a national security issue of enormous proportions and also a significant failure in the federal bureaucracy." Democrats indicated they would not let up on investigating any potential national security risks when they seize control of the House and Senate in January. "The Trump Administration’s rush to reinstate Jensen Huang underscores the need for Congress to act," Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said in a statement. "Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasizing that he’s learned nothing from his resounding election defeat." Schumer said Democrats will "wield their full power" to investigate any wrongdoing by Huang, Nvidia and the Trump administration. "We'll also work on a bipartisan basis to continue advancing policies that stop the flow of our most powerful technology to the Chinese military and other adversaries." Congressional leaders already plan to investigate whether Huang's relationship constituted a national security breach. 1, Huang is scheduled to testify in closed-door meetings with three Republican-led congressional committees. Tim Scott, chairman of the Senate Banking Committee, announced that Huang would also testify in a public hearing on Dec. Export Controls.” Meanwhile, in California, Atty. Rob Bonta said that the state Department of Justice would continue its investigation into whether confidential information or advanced chips were sent to China as well as whether Nvidia issued statements that misled investors or the public. “It’s wrong, and it’s shocking,” Bonta said of Huang's reinstatement. “And it raises a lot of red flags and questions about tech oligarchy and the president and his involvement, interference, manipulation with this decision and whether, if and how national security is being put at risk.” Huang resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive on Nov. 12, after reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a Singapore-based businesswoman suspected by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese spy. “I can’t wait to get back to work,” Huang said in a statement Monday. “I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution. I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment." Harvey C. Jones, chair of the board, said the board believed Huang is the right person to lead Nvidia. “His reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” Jones said in a statement. "We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company." Nvidia's market value plummeted over the last month, prompting widespread concerns about the durability of the tech sector and the overall U.S. economy. Still, during the company's earnings call last week, interim Chief Executive Colette Kress and members of Nvidia's board stressed that it was unlikely Huang would return: his actions, they said, did not align with the company’s code of conduct. Huang's reinstatement came after Trump said Friday that he and Chinese President Xi Jinping briefly discussed their shared respect for Huang during Trump's trip to Asia last week. “I did discuss that with President Xi, and he said, ‘Oh, brilliant, brilliant. And I think the company, if they were smart, they’d take that brilliant man, accept an apology and let him go back to work,” Trump said at a White House news conference. On Sunday evening, Trump wrote on Truth Social that he hoped that the board of Nvidia would rehire Huang. "It would be the best thing for the Company," he wrote, "and also, for the U.S.A." Jacob Bourne, an analyst at Emarketer, called Huang’s reinstatement "a stunning new development, but not an altogether surprising one." "After more than three decades at the helm, Huang has become so central to Nvidia’s identity and the broader AI trade that his departure fueled uncertainty during an already volatile period for the industry," Bourne said in a statement. "His return may help restore investor confidence, but the upheaval echoes Sam Altman’s brief ouster and reinstatement at OpenAI, raising similar questions about corporate governance and the outsized influence of individual leaders over the future of AI." Beyond that, Ramesh Srinivasan, director of the UC Center for Global Digital Cultures, said the episode reflects how central Nvidia has become to the AI economy and thus the economy overall — in part thanks to the federal government’s investments in it — and the Trump administration’s attempt to reassure markets in order to keep backstopping it. “Look at the incredible volatility we’ve seen with the S&P 500 and look in particular at the volatility we’ve seen with the Nvidia stock," Srinivasan said. "I think that this is an attempt to inject some sort of stability in what’s clearly an unstable situation with that stock, and that’s why we’ve seen the short term rebounds.” “Whether we like it or not as consumers, workers, citizens, Nvidia has been set up as just a critical part, a central part of the whole AI game, the whole AI investment, the whole AI economy, and that’s because they are the central chip maker,” he added. According to Angela Zhang, a USC law professor and expert on Chinese tech regulation, Huang’s return and Trump's political intervention provided additional evidence that in “its effort to contain China, America is increasingly beginning to resemble China.” “The market’s enthusiastic response to Trump’s intervention and Jensen Huang’s return may appear to signal a happy outcome in the short term," Zhang wrote on LinkedIn. "But beneath that immediate optimism lies a more troubling question: What does this mean for the long-term integrity of American corporate governance and the rule of law in its financial markets?

sources.title: Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO, board chair
passages: Nvidia’s board of directors has voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO and chairman of the board, just 11 days after he resigned in the wake of multiple scandals .
President Trump has also been a major backer of Huang’s return to Nvidia.

Appearing on CNBC Monday morning , Trump said that he had spoken to the Nvidia board “directly and indirectly” about Huang’s reinstatement, and that Huang “did nothing wrong.” Losing “the brainpower of someone like [Huang]” would be “a much bigger threat” than anything related to his alleged interactions with China, Trump said.

That assurance comes despite Huang’s admitted affair with a woman who, US intelligence sources believe, was working as a Chinese spy and allegations that Nvidia had subverted export controls meant to keep Nvidia chips from reaching China.

extraction.body: Trump says he spoke to the board and that Huang “did nothing wrong.” Nvidia’s board of directors has voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO and chairman of the board, just 11 days after he resigned in the wake of multiple scandals . The reinstatement, announced Monday morning , is “effective immediately” and was based in part on “input from senior levels of the United States government” that assured the board members that “Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” That assurance comes despite Huang’s admitted affair with a woman who, US intelligence sources believe, was working as a Chinese spy and allegations that Nvidia had subverted export controls meant to keep Nvidia chips from reaching China. It also comes despite multiple developing investigations from multiple different government departments into those and other alleged national security, accounting, and corporate governance failures. Huang had been seeking a return to Nvidia since shortly after his resignation, reportedly forming a war room to strategize how best to bring it to pass. Last week, Huang posted on social media that “if the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” President Trump has also been a major backer of Huang’s return to Nvidia. “I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang,” he wrote on Truth Social last week. “It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A.” In a social media post immediately following the reinstatement, Trump called it “the correct and proper decision” and confirmed that “the United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.” Appearing on CNBC Monday morning , Trump said that he had spoken to the Nvidia board “directly and indirectly” about Huang’s reinstatement, and that Huang “did nothing wrong.” Losing “the brainpower of someone like [Huang]” would be “a much bigger threat” than anything related to his alleged interactions with China, Trump said. “We’ve done a very thorough investigation and the investigation showed that… he had bad judgement having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents,” Trump said. “You have to protect our geniuses and there aren’t enough of them.” Huang’s tenure at Nvidia dates back to the company’s founding in 1993, when he and three cofounders were focused on the then-nascent field of GPU hardware aimed at PC gamers. In the decades since, the highly parallel cores in those GPUs have been embraced first by cryptocurrency miners and then AI companies, propelling the company to its position as the most valuable in the world at its October peak. Nvidia stock—the price of which had sunk roughly 25 percent since Huang’s resignation was announced and nearly 50 percent since its peak—was up about 30 percent in early morning trading in the immediate aftermath of Huang’s reinstatement announcement. Huang’s return echoes, in some ways, that of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who was fired almost exactly three years ago after the board said it “no longer has confidence in his ability to continue leading OpenAI.” Two weeks later, Altman was back at the helm after many employees threatened a mass revolt and departure if he wasn’t brought back. In Huang’s case, the revolt following his departure came not from employees but from fellow titans of the tech industry. Executives including Altman, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, xAI’s Elon Musk and Anduril’s Palmer Luckey are among the prominent industry figures who have publicly offered him support in the days since his resignation. In its statement, the Nvidia board reiterated that it has retained independent counsel and formed a committee of independent directors to investigate what it calls Huang’s targeting by “a foreign intelligence effort.” The company has also formed a National Security and Export Control Committee to “oversee trade compliance and national security risks,” and is seeking to hire a new chief compliance officer. This story has been updated to reflect Trump’s statements to CNBC.

“I’ve been speaking to the board directly and indirectly, and I felt very strongly about it,” Trump said.

Trump also expressed concern that if Huang was not reinstated, China could try to recruit him to work for a Chinese company.

“The bigger impact was, you know, he’s got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about, including me.” The president initially supported the idea of former Apple CEO Tim Cook being brought on to run Nvidia before he endorsed Huang’s return.
Trump told CNBC that he did not think “anybody can do” what Huang does, referring to the company’s prospects moving forward.
“If we didn’t do this, I could see China coming in and saying to Jensen, “Hey, how would you like to come to China?” Trump said.

Huang’s reinstatement at the top of Nvidia sent stocks surging after the market slid last week.
“I think Tim would have helped revive the stock, but I don’t think anybody could revive the stock like it’s being revived right now,” Trump said.

Huang’s reinstatement at the top of Nvidia sent stocks surging after the market slid last week. In the nearly hourlong interview, Trump cast himself as a central figure in Huang’s reinstatement, saying he spoke with the key players involved in the company. The president added that he spoke with Huang “after I made the deal, after the deal was finished.” “I called him up and I said, ‘I ask you to do one thing, Jensen, work hard,’” Trump said. “I didn’t talk about other things because he understands that. Trump said on CNBC that the administration assured the company that Huang, who allegedly had an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy, did not pose a national security risk. “One of the things the board wanted to know, is there a national security problem?” Trump said. “And after a lot of research, we — you know, we’ve been looking at this for more than a couple of days, right? We said no, it’s not a problem.” Later in the interview, Trump took credit more directly for Huang’s reinstatement. Asked on CNBC whether he thought Huang would have been rehired without his intervention, Trump said, “I believe my intervention was very important.” When asked what he told the board to convince them to reinstate Huang, Trump said he changed the board’s minds. “I spoke to them, let me just put it that way, and I convinced them, and I must tell you, it was a lot easier to convince them yesterday than it was a week and a half ago,” the president said, pointing to the company’s stock price diving in the wake of the scandal and shake-up. The reinstatement comes less than two weeks after Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia following reports that he was in an extramarital relationship with a woman alleged to be a spy for the Chinese government and reports of a second affair with an executive who was his direct subordinate at the company. Trump, who has staunchly defended Huang and denied reports that he received a U.S. intelligence briefing last spring on the CEO’s alleged involvement with a Beijing operative, said he “convinced” the board to reinstate Huang. “I spoke to them, let me put it that way,” the president said in a phone interview on CNBC shortly after the board announced Huang’s immediate return as CEO, president and member of the board. “And I convinced them.” Trump said Vice President JD Vance, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick were also part of those decisions. The board said it received input from “senior levels of the United States government” on the decision to reinstate Huang, and was “confident” that Huang posed no national security risk. Vance helped spearhead the effort to convince the board that Huang would pose no national security risk if reinstalled atop the influential company, which has been the primary provider of the chips that have powered the data center boom for the last year. The Wall Street Journal, citing a U.S. official with knowledge of the matter that that Vance held talks with board members over the weekend. The vice president worked in Silicon Valley before entering politics, where he became a mentee of PayPal co-founder Peter Thiel and made connections with other prominent tech billionaires who have helped fund his path to power in Washington. Trump told CNBC that reports of Huang’s affairs received intense scrutiny not because of the potential for tremendous national security implications but because “sex sells.” “It could be a net positive,” Trump said. They respect it.”The New York Times reported in October that Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the drafting of an intelligence memo last spring that warned Trump and his top Cabinet officials of U.S. intelligence assessments that the businesswoman, who goes by the name Alice Huang, was believed to be a spy. Trump denied having seen that memo in remarks to reporters earlier this month and said he did not know about the national security concerns when he invited Huang to join him on a trip to China in May. Trump said the Nvidia board “made the correct and proper decision” by reinstating Huang in a post on Truth Social on Monday. “The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy,” Trump said. “The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.” Trump added that Attorney General Todd Blanche “has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that [Huang] has engaged in any unlawful conduct.” A senior administration official with direct knowledge of the matter who was granted anonymity to dicuss internal matters said the Justice Department did not get a heads-up about Huang's reinstatement. The official said the department's probe into Singapore-based Megaspeed, where the alleged spy was a top executive and which bought Nvidia chips, remains ongoing. In a subsequent post, the president shared an image generated by artificial intelligence of a bloodied Huang triumphantly hoisting a bright red bra in the air. John Cornyn of Texas said, “You gotta be kidding me!" "Jensen Huang was compromised and exploited by a Chinese spy," Rep. "Nvidia should have moved on without Huang and ignored the administration’s inexplicable desire to save Huang," adding that "Congress needs to get to the bottom of who approved high-end computer chips sales to China." Huang is slated to testify before Congress next month amid concern that Alice Huang was using her role at Megaspeed, which has purchased billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia’s most advanced AI chip, to divert the technology to China. Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C., announced on Monday that a hearing titled "Protecting America's AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Lutnick has faced bipartisan scrutiny on Capitol Hill for his reported failure to blacklist Megaspeed from purchasing the advanced chips. The department abruptly stopped an investigation into the company last year and transferred the case to the Justice Department. The commerce secretary has mirrored Huang’s friendly position on the export of advanced AI chips to China, clashing at times with top Trump administration officials who have sought strict export controls on the technology. He has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee as concerns rise that he prioritized private tech companies’ interests over national security. Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said Monday: "Mr. Huang’s sudden reinstatement at NVIDIA this week, reportedly at the encouragement of Trump Administration officials and without any apparent accounting or response to the risks to our national security, demands an explanation. Huang to still appear before Congress, but we also need full accountability of the actions of the Trump Administration and cabinet officials.” Mychael Schnell and Paula Reid contributed to this report.

“It’s wrong, and it’s shocking,” Bonta said of Huang's reinstatement.

extraction.body: Less than two weeks after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after his extramarital affair raised national security concerns, Nvidia's board announced Monday that it had reinstated him as president and chief executive “effective immediately." Nvidia's board of directors voted unanimously to reinstate Huang after a series of discussions and meetings with him, Nvidia said in a statement, noting that the board received input from senior levels of the U.S. government. “Based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” President Trump signaled he strongly supported Huang's reinstatement. In an interview with CNBC, he declared Nvidia had been "exonerated" and on social media said the company had made an “absolutely GREAT decision.” "The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy," Trump said on Truth Social. Trump said the U.S. attorney general had confirmed the government does not possess evidence that Huang engaged in unlawful conduct. He added he had "gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure." The news sent Nvidia stock soaring nearly 30%, regaining most of its losses. But as tech leaders and venture capitalists rejoiced — “The mistake has been corrected,” billionaire tech leader Elon Musk posted on X — prominent lawmakers in Washington, on both sides of the political aisle, expressed skepticism about Huang's reinstatement and called for more congressional oversight. Newt Gingrich, the former Republican speaker of the House, posted on X that there was something "profoundly wrong" with Huang having a relationship with a Chinese spy and helping China get advanced computer chips. "Congress should really dig into this as a national security issue of enormous proportions and also a significant failure in the federal bureaucracy." Democrats indicated they would not let up on investigating any potential national security risks when they seize control of the House and Senate in January. "The Trump Administration’s rush to reinstate Jensen Huang underscores the need for Congress to act," Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said in a statement. "Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasizing that he’s learned nothing from his resounding election defeat." Schumer said Democrats will "wield their full power" to investigate any wrongdoing by Huang, Nvidia and the Trump administration. "We'll also work on a bipartisan basis to continue advancing policies that stop the flow of our most powerful technology to the Chinese military and other adversaries." Congressional leaders already plan to investigate whether Huang's relationship constituted a national security breach. 1, Huang is scheduled to testify in closed-door meetings with three Republican-led congressional committees. Tim Scott, chairman of the Senate Banking Committee, announced that Huang would also testify in a public hearing on Dec. Export Controls.” Meanwhile, in California, Atty. Rob Bonta said that the state Department of Justice would continue its investigation into whether confidential information or advanced chips were sent to China as well as whether Nvidia issued statements that misled investors or the public. “It’s wrong, and it’s shocking,” Bonta said of Huang's reinstatement. “And it raises a lot of red flags and questions about tech oligarchy and the president and his involvement, interference, manipulation with this decision and whether, if and how national security is being put at risk.” Huang resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive on Nov. 12, after reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a Singapore-based businesswoman suspected by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese spy. “I can’t wait to get back to work,” Huang said in a statement Monday. “I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution. I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment." Harvey C. Jones, chair of the board, said the board believed Huang is the right person to lead Nvidia. “His reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” Jones said in a statement. "We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company." Nvidia's market value plummeted over the last month, prompting widespread concerns about the durability of the tech sector and the overall U.S. economy. Still, during the company's earnings call last week, interim Chief Executive Colette Kress and members of Nvidia's board stressed that it was unlikely Huang would return: his actions, they said, did not align with the company’s code of conduct. Huang's reinstatement came after Trump said Friday that he and Chinese President Xi Jinping briefly discussed their shared respect for Huang during Trump's trip to Asia last week. “I did discuss that with President Xi, and he said, ‘Oh, brilliant, brilliant. And I think the company, if they were smart, they’d take that brilliant man, accept an apology and let him go back to work,” Trump said at a White House news conference. On Sunday evening, Trump wrote on Truth Social that he hoped that the board of Nvidia would rehire Huang. "It would be the best thing for the Company," he wrote, "and also, for the U.S.A." Jacob Bourne, an analyst at Emarketer, called Huang’s reinstatement "a stunning new development, but not an altogether surprising one." sources.title: Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO, board chair
passages: Nvidia’s board of directors has voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO and chairman of the board, just 11 days after he resigned in the wake of multiple scandals .
President Trump has also been a major backer of Huang’s return to Nvidia.

Appearing on CNBC Monday morning , Trump said that he had spoken to the Nvidia board “directly and indirectly” about Huang’s reinstatement, and that Huang “did nothing wrong.” Losing “the brainpower of someone like [Huang]” would be “a much bigger threat” than anything related to his alleged interactions with China, Trump said.

That assurance comes despite Huang’s admitted affair with a woman who, US intelligence sources believe, was working as a Chinese spy and allegations that Nvidia had subverted export controls meant to keep Nvidia chips from reaching China.

extraction.body: Trump says he spoke to the board and that Huang “did nothing wrong.” Nvidia’s board of directors has voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO and chairman of the board, just 11 days after he resigned in the wake of multiple scandals . The reinstatement, announced Monday morning , is “effective immediately” and was based in part on “input from senior levels of the United States government” that assured the board members that “Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” That assurance comes despite Huang’s admitted affair with a woman who, US intelligence sources believe, was working as a Chinese spy and allegations that Nvidia had subverted export controls meant to keep Nvidia chips from reaching China. It also comes despite multiple developing investigations from multiple different government departments into those and other alleged national security, accounting, and corporate governance failures. Huang had been seeking a return to Nvidia since shortly after his resignation, reportedly forming a war room to strategize how best to bring it to pass. Last week, Huang posted on social media that “if the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” President Trump has also been a major backer of Huang’s return to Nvidia. “I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang,” he wrote on Truth Social last week. “It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A.” In a social media post immediately following the reinstatement, Trump called it “the correct and proper decision” and confirmed that “the United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.” Appearing on CNBC Monday morning , Trump said that he had spoken to the Nvidia board “directly and indirectly” about Huang’s reinstatement, and that Huang “did nothing wrong.” Losing “the brainpower of someone like [Huang]” would be “a much bigger threat” than anything related to his alleged interactions with China, Trump said. “We’ve done a very thorough investigation and the investigation showed that… he had bad judgement having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents,” Trump said. “You have to protect our geniuses and there aren’t enough of them.” Huang’s tenure at Nvidia dates back to the company’s founding in 1993, when he and three cofounders were focused on the then-nascent field of GPU hardware aimed at PC gamers. In the decades since, the highly parallel cores in those GPUs have been embraced first by cryptocurrency miners and then AI companies, propelling the company to its position as the most valuable in the world at its October peak. Nvidia stock—the price of which had sunk roughly 25 percent since Huang’s resignation was announced and nearly 50 percent since its peak—was up about 30 percent in early morning trading in the immediate aftermath of Huang’s reinstatement announcement. Huang’s return echoes, in some ways, that of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who was fired almost exactly three years ago after the board said it “no longer has confidence in his ability to continue leading OpenAI.” Two weeks later, Altman was back at the helm after many employees threatened a mass revolt and departure if he wasn’t brought back. In Huang’s case, the revolt following his departure came not from employees but from fellow titans of the tech industry. Executives including Altman, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, xAI’s Elon Musk and Anduril’s Palmer Luckey are among the prominent industry figures who have publicly offered him support in the days since his resignation. In its statement, the Nvidia board reiterated that it has retained independent counsel and formed a committee of independent directors to investigate what it calls Huang’s targeting by “a foreign intelligence effort.” The company has also formed a National Security and Export Control Committee to “oversee trade compliance and national security risks,” and is seeking to hire a new chief compliance officer. This story has been updated to reflect Trump’s statements to CNBC.

Trump also expressed concern that if Huang was not reinstated, China could try to recruit him to work for a Chinese company.

“The bigger impact was, you know, he’s got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about, including me.” The president initially supported the idea of former Apple CEO Tim Cook being brought on to run Nvidia before he endorsed Huang’s return.

Huang’s reinstatement at the top of Nvidia sent stocks surging after the market slid last week. In the nearly hourlong interview, Trump cast himself as a central figure in Huang’s reinstatement, saying he spoke with the key players involved in the company. The president added that he spoke with Huang “after I made the deal, after the deal was finished.” “I called him up and I said, ‘I ask you to do one thing, Jensen, work hard,’” Trump said. “I didn’t talk about other things because he understands that. He knows what to do and what not to do.” Earlier Monday, Nvidia said in a statement that it had received assurances about Huang from the U.S. government, though it did not name Trump. “In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk,” the board said. Trump said on CNBC that the administration assured the company that Huang, who allegedly had an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy, did not pose a national security risk. “One of the things the board wanted to know, is there a national security problem?” Trump said. “And after a lot of research, we — you know, we’ve been looking at this for more than a couple of days, right? We said no, it’s not a problem.” Later in the interview, Trump took credit more directly for Huang’s reinstatement. Asked on CNBC whether he thought Huang would have been rehired without his intervention, Trump said, “I believe my intervention was very important.” When asked what he told the board to convince them to reinstate Huang, Trump said he changed the board’s minds. “I spoke to them, let me just put it that way, and I convinced them, and I must tell you, it was a lot easier to convince them yesterday than it was a week and a half ago,” the president said, pointing to the company’s stock price diving in the wake of the scandal and shake-up. In the interview, Trump also said “basically I was represented at the board.” Asked whether last week’s stock market losses affected his view on Huang’s return to Nvidia, Trump said, “probably so.” “But the bigger impact was the long term,” Trump said. “The bigger impact was, you know, he’s got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about, including me.” The president initially supported the idea of former Apple CEO Tim Cook being brought on to run Nvidia before he endorsed Huang’s return. Nvidia’s stock shot up and markets rebounded after the board’s announcement of Huang’s return. Trump also expressed concern that if Huang was not reinstated, China could try to recruit him to work for a Chinese company. “If we didn’t do this, I could see China coming in and saying to Jensen, “Hey, how would you like to come to China?” Trump said. Don Bacon, R-Neb., said Nvidia should have “ignored the Administration’s inexplicable desire to save Huang.” Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., accused the president of “selling out our national security to keep the stock market high.” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, meanwhile, foreshadowed congressional investigations when Democrats take control of Congress in the new year. “Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain,” Schumer, D-N.Y., said in the post. The reinstatement comes less than two weeks after Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia following reports that he was in an extramarital relationship with a woman alleged to be a spy for the Chinese government and reports of a second affair with an executive who was his direct subordinate at the company. Trump, who has staunchly defended Huang and denied reports that he received a U.S. intelligence briefing last spring on the CEO’s alleged involvement with a Beijing operative, said he “convinced” the board to reinstate Huang. “I spoke to them, let me put it that way,” the president said in a phone interview on CNBC shortly after the board announced Huang’s immediate return as CEO, president and member of the board. “And I convinced them.” Trump said Vice President JD Vance, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick were also part of those decisions. The board said it received input from “senior levels of the United States government” on the decision to reinstate Huang, and was “confident” that Huang posed no national security risk. Vance helped spearhead the effort to convince the board that Huang would pose no national security risk if reinstalled atop the influential company, which has been the primary provider of the chips that have powered the data center boom for the last year. The Wall Street Journal, citing a U.S. official with knowledge of the matter that that Vance held talks with board members over the weekend. The vice president worked in Silicon Valley before entering politics, where he became a mentee of PayPal co-founder Peter Thiel and made connections with other prominent tech billionaires who have helped fund his path to power in Washington. Trump told CNBC that reports of Huang’s affairs received intense scrutiny not because of the potential for tremendous national security implications but because “sex sells.” “It could be a net positive,” Trump said. They respect it.”The New York Times reported in October that Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the drafting of an intelligence memo last spring that warned Trump and his top Cabinet officials of U.S. intelligence assessments that the businesswoman, who goes by the name Alice Huang, was believed to be a spy. Trump denied having seen that memo in remarks to reporters earlier this month and said he did not know about the national security concerns when he invited Huang to join him on a trip to China in May. Trump said the Nvidia board “made the correct and proper decision” by reinstating Huang in a post on Truth Social on Monday. “The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy,” Trump said. “The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.” Trump added that Attorney General Todd Blanche “has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that [Huang] has engaged in any unlawful conduct.” A senior administration official with direct knowledge of the matter who was granted anonymity to dicuss internal matters said the Justice Department did not get a heads-up about Huang's reinstatement. The official said the department's probe into Singapore-based Megaspeed, where the alleged spy was a top executive and which bought Nvidia chips, remains ongoing. In a subsequent post, the president shared an image generated by artificial intelligence of a bloodied Huang triumphantly hoisting a bright red bra in the air. The image mimics the iconic photograph of Trump hoisting his fist in the air after surviving an assassination attempt during a rally for his 2024 presidential campaign in Butler, Pennsylvania. In the fake image, a flag with the Nvidia logo takes the place of the American flag that waves in the background of the real photo. Trump told CNBC he “was represented at the board,” adding that he would “rather not say, you know, who I spoke to.” The decision was a stunning reversal from the board’s previous stance. Harvey Jones, the chair, said on Nvidia’s earnings call last week that the board had no intention of reinstating Huang. Nvidia shares surged more than 30% in New York on Monday following the news of Huang’s return. Republicans slammed the company's decision to reinstate Huang as CEO. John Cornyn of Texas said, “You gotta be kidding me!" "Jensen Huang was compromised and exploited by a Chinese spy," Rep. "Nvidia should have moved on without Huang and ignored the administration’s inexplicable desire to save Huang," adding that "Congress needs to get to the bottom of who approved high-end computer chips sales to China." Huang is slated to testify before Congress next month amid concern that Alice Huang was using her role at Megaspeed, which has purchased billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia’s most advanced AI chip, to divert the technology to China. Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C., announced on Monday that a hearing titled "Protecting America's AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Lutnick has faced bipartisan scrutiny on Capitol Hill for his reported failure to blacklist Megaspeed from purchasing the advanced chips. The department abruptly stopped an investigation into the company last year and transferred the case to the Justice Department. The commerce secretary has mirrored Huang’s friendly position on the export of advanced AI chips to China, clashing at times with top Trump administration officials who have sought strict export controls on the technology. He has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee as concerns rise that he prioritized private tech companies’ interests over national security. Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said Monday: "Mr. Huang’s sudden reinstatement at NVIDIA this week, reportedly at the encouragement of Trump Administration officials and without any apparent accounting or response to the risks to our national security, demands an explanation. Huang to still appear before Congress, but we also need full accountability of the actions of the Trump Administration and cabinet officials.” Mychael Schnell and Paula Reid contributed to this report.

extraction.body: Nvidia has reinstated CEO Jensen Huang just days after rejecting his offer to return to the AI chipmaker - and less than two weeks after he was forced to resign over reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. The company had come under pressure from Donald Trump to reappoint Huang - and on Monday, the US president said he "made the deal" to "convince" the tech giant's board to reverse course and bring Huang back. But Democrats have accused the Trump administration of selling out national security for financial gain. Huang is due to testify before Congress in early December. His comeback helped end a week-long losing streak in US stocks that had left the S&P 500 in correction territory. Stock prices for Nvidia fell sharply after Huang stepped down, but jumped by 31% after he was reappointed on Monday - adding about $1tn to the company's market value. But Nvidia's closing price was still down slightly from its Friday morning opening price. Board Chairman Harvey C Jones said in a statement earlier in the day: "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers." The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk. It was only last Tuesday that the board explicitly said it did not intend to reinstate him. Huang resigned from Nvidia on 12 November following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman, Alice Huang, who was alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence. On Monday, the US Commerce Department announced it was preparing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer where Alice Huang was CEO. In a brief interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump said he had spoken to Nvidia's board of directors and "convinced" them to bring back Huang. Trump praised the Nvidia board for acting "really responsibly" in reinstating the CEO. "They did ask for assurance on the national security threat," Trump said. "And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot." "People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it's a threat to lose him," the president added. The president was asked whether Nvidia stock losses after Huang resigned last week had influenced his decision to personally intervene. The head of the International Association for Safe and Ethical AI told the BBC that the Nvidia board must have been under "enormous pressure" from the White House to reinstate Huang. Prof Stuart Russell, who is professor of computer science at UC Berkeley, said the stock price of Nvidia and similar firms has been a major factor in "underpinning US economic growth for years". "I assume the White House was worried that the markets would go down a lot further in the next few weeks unless they go him back in," he says. Trump's vocal backing of Huang comes despite the concerns of US lawmakers, including some Republicans, over the CEO's affair and Nvidia's compliance with US export controls. "Nvidia should have moved on without Huang and ignored the administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang," Republican congressman Don Bacon of Nebraska said. "We cannot say we want to win the AI race and then give China our best technology. We need sunlight on who is responsible." Sen Tom Cotton, fellow Republican who represents Arkansas, vowed that Congress would investigate. "The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back," he said. Democrats, who will control both chambers of Congress from January, have already promised to launch Nvidia investigations. Two days later, he has been asked to testify before the Senate banking committee. Since returning last year to the White House, Trump has amassed a significant level of investment in Nvidia. Recent financial disclosures show he purchased $265,000 in its stock and sold as much as $15,000 worth of shares in September. A BBC review of his government financial disclosures for the last two years shows he purchased shares of Nvidia stock worth between $23m and $86m (£18m and £66m). And he has bought Nvidia stock 85 separate times through a number of investment accounts. The value of those holdings would have been affected by the recent fall in Nvidia's stock price amid Huang's exit. Trump has also sold some of his stake in Nvidia since returning to the presidency. Over 19 sales, Trump gained between $3.5m and $10.2m, according to his government disclosures. Both Trump and White House have repeatedly rejected assertions that he has profited from the presidency. The president has said "everybody" was making money from rising stocks and he does not make decisions related to his investment accounts. The White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons. The US Army has moved its plans to detonate five tonnes of toxic explosives to Wednesday. passages: President Donald Trump has expressed his support for NVIDIA’s decision to reinstate founder Jensen Huang as Chief Executive Officer, stating that the U.S. government has no reason to believe his return poses a national security risk and holds no evidence that he engaged in unlawful conduct.

Trump made the remarks on Monday, November 23, 2026, in a post on his social media platform, Truth Social , following NVIDIA’s announcement that Huang had been reinstated as President, CEO, and a member of the Board of Directors after stepping down earlier in November.

As Jensen Huang resumes his leadership responsibilities, NVIDIA faces the challenge of maintaining its position in the expanding AI market while strengthening safeguards for sensitive information and ensuring compliance with U.S. regulations.
According to TechCrunch, Alice Huang worked as an executive at Megaspeed , a Singapore-based company that had purchased billions of dollars’ worth of NVIDIA chips over the previous several years.
The reports also included allegations of other personal relationships involving Huang and NVIDIA employees, including one employee who reportedly reported directly to him.
When asked whether he meant Huang would be reinstated as NVIDIA CEO, Trump responded that he hoped so.
These remarks reflect Trump’s position on the matter, rather than a formal determination regarding the allegations or the outcome of any investigation.

Trump made the remarks on Monday, November 23, 2026, in a post on his social media platform, Truth Social , following NVIDIA’s announcement that Huang had been reinstated as President, CEO, and a member of the Board of Directors after stepping down earlier in November.

As Jensen Huang resumes his leadership responsibilities, NVIDIA faces the challenge of maintaining its position in the expanding AI market while strengthening safeguards for sensitive information and ensuring compliance with U.S. regulations.
According to TechCrunch, Alice Huang worked as an executive at Megaspeed , a Singapore-based company that had purchased billions of dollars’ worth of NVIDIA chips over the previous several years.
The reports also included allegations of other personal relationships involving Huang and NVIDIA employees, including one employee who reportedly reported directly to him.
When asked whether he meant Huang would be reinstated as NVIDIA CEO, Trump responded that he hoped so.
These remarks reflect Trump’s position on the matter, rather than a formal determination regarding the allegations or the outcome of any investigation.

Trump made the remarks on Monday, November 23, 2026, in a post on his social media platform, Truth Social , following NVIDIA’s announcement that Huang had been reinstated as President, CEO, and a member of the Board of Directors after stepping down earlier in November. The president described the board’s decision as the right move, emphasizing the importance of Huang’s leadership not only to NVIDIA but also to the broader U.S. economy. In his Truth Social statement, Trump said the U.S. government had no reason to believe that Jensen Huang’s reinstatement would threaten national security. He also claimed that U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche had confirmed the government possessed no evidence that Huang had engaged in unlawful conduct. However, these claims were made by Trump, and Blanche had not issued a separate formal statement on the case at the time of TechCrunch’s report . Trump’s comments drew attention because federal criminal investigations are generally handled by the Department of Justice through its established legal processes. Meanwhile, NVIDIA’s Board of Directors confirmed that it had consulted senior U.S. government officials before deciding to reinstate Huang. According to the company, the information received during those consultations supported the board’s conclusion that Huang’s return would not pose a national security risk. Comments Trump made over the weekend suggest he may have been aware of discussions surrounding Huang’s potential reinstatement before NVIDIA officially announced its decision. Speaking to a PBS journalist, Trump indicated that Huang was back where he belonged and expressed his belief that the executive had done nothing wrong. When asked whether he meant Huang would be reinstated as NVIDIA CEO, Trump responded that he hoped so. The remarks came before NVIDIA formally confirmed Huang’s return, raising questions about how much the administration knew about the discussions preceding the board’s decision. However, Trump’s statements alone do not establish that he had advance knowledge of the final decision or its announcement date. The controversy stems from media reports concerning Huang’s personal relationships, including one involving Alice Huang , a woman whom U.S. officials reportedly suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence. Despite sharing the same surname, Alice Huang is not related to NVIDIA’s CEO. According to TechCrunch, Alice Huang worked as an executive at Megaspeed , a Singapore-based company that had purchased billions of dollars’ worth of NVIDIA chips over the previous several years. The reported relationship raised national security concerns about whether sensitive company information could have been compromised or whether Huang’s connection to Alice Huang could have facilitated China’s access to advanced U.S. AI chips subject to export restrictions. The reports also included allegations of other personal relationships involving Huang and NVIDIA employees, including one employee who reportedly reported directly to him. However, the allegations do not establish that Alice Huang worked for Chinese intelligence or that Jensen Huang disclosed sensitive information or helped circumvent U.S. export restrictions. The president further referred to the broader intelligence rivalry between the United States and China. These remarks reflect Trump’s position on the matter, rather than a formal determination regarding the allegations or the outcome of any investigation. Despite supporting Jensen Huang’s reinstatement, Trump emphasized that NVIDIA should continue its internal investigation into compliance with U.S. export controls. He urged the company to ensure that it meets its legal obligations concerning the export of advanced semiconductor technology and the protection of U.S. national security. NVIDIA’s Board of Directors has also confirmed that its independent investigation into reports of a foreign intelligence effort targeting Huang will continue despite his return. The company has established a National Security and Export Control Committee , consisting entirely of independent board members, to oversee national security risks and trade compliance. However, presidential support does not replace independent investigative procedures or NVIDIA’s obligations under U.S. national security and export control regulations. Trump’s endorsement represents a significant political development following NVIDIA’s decision to restore Jensen Huang to the CEO position after his brief departure. Although Trump stated that the U.S. government had no evidence of unlawful conduct by Huang, NVIDIA’s independent investigation remains ongoing. The investigation’s findings, along with the company’s newly introduced national security and export compliance measures, will remain important factors in the case. As Jensen Huang resumes his leadership responsibilities, NVIDIA faces the challenge of maintaining its position in the expanding AI market while strengthening safeguards for sensitive information and ensuring compliance with U.S. regulations.

extraction.body: The Trump administration on Monday added Megaspeed to a trade blacklist that would prevent the company from obtaining U.S.-made semiconductors and other tech products after the company was linked to the Nvidia scandal. Megaspeed's addition to the Commerce Department's entity list bars U.S. tech companies from providing goods, software and technology to Megaspeed without receiving a license. The Singapore-based company specializes in providing computing power for data centers training AI models. Nvidia's website lists Megaspeed as a preferred cloud partner. The company's addition to the Commerce Department's entity list comes after former executive Alice Huang, who is alleged to be a spy for Beijing, had an extramarital relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who was reinstated to his role on Monday. SHORT SELLER FLAGGED JENSEN HUANG'S 'UNCOMFORTABLY CLOSE' TIES TO ALLEGED CHINESE SPY MONTHS AGO Megaspeed previously faced an investigation by the U.S. government as regulators probed whether the company was helping Chinese customers obtain advanced AI chips made by Nvidia that are covered by export controls. FOX Business reached out to Megaspeed and the Commerce Department for comment. The Commerce Department and Justice Department released a joint statement on Nov. 16 explaining that Commerce opened its probe into Megaspeed in 2024 for potential export control violations. WHAT JENSEN HUANG'S RETURN MEANS FOR NVIDIA – AND WALL STREET In May 2025, the agency's investigators requested records from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed, and a month later, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its "no sell" list. Also in June 2025, agents from Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security worked with Singaporean law enforcement officials to conduct an onsite, in-person end-use check at Megaspeed and interviewed Alice Huang, who was CEO at the time. Following those actions, the Justice Department took the lead in a criminal investigation of Megaspeed and the agencies are working together to "bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred." NVIDIA REINSTATES JENSEN HUANG AS CEO EFFECTIVE IMMEDIATELY FOLLOWING US GOVERNMENT INPUT "Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the U.S. economy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce will remain vigilant in pursuing justice for those who want to compromise America's technological edge," the agencies said in their Nov. Megaspeed CEO James Tan Yong Pong said in a Nov. 12 statement that the company "takes its compliance obligations under U.S. export control laws extremely seriously.

Megaspeed's addition to the Commerce Department's entity list bars U.S. tech companies from providing goods, software and technology to Megaspeed without receiving a license. The Singapore-based company specializes in providing computing power for data centers training AI models. Nvidia's website lists Megaspeed as a preferred cloud partner. The company's addition to the Commerce Department's entity list comes after former executive Alice Huang, who is alleged to be a spy for Beijing, had an extramarital relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who was reinstated to his role on Monday. FOX Business reached out to Megaspeed and the Commerce Department for comment. The Commerce Department and Justice Department released a joint statement on Nov. 16 explaining that Commerce opened its probe into Megaspeed in 2024 for potential export control violations. WHAT JENSEN HUANG'S RETURN MEANS FOR NVIDIA – AND WALL STREET In May 2025, the agency's investigators requested records from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed, and a month later, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its "no sell" list. Also in June 2025, agents from Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security worked with Singaporean law enforcement officials to conduct an onsite, in-person end-use check at Megaspeed and interviewed Alice Huang, who was CEO at the time. Six days ago the board’s chair, Harvey Jones, said the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” President Trump urged the board to rehire Huang early Monday, The Washington Post reported, and Nvidia’s release followed at 8:55 a.m. ET. Besides the job title, the release makes three changes. A new board committee. Nvidia is forming a National Security and Export Control Committee made up of independent directors. Export rules already decide which chips Nvidia may sell in China, and that subject now gets its own group of directors. For shareholders, the thing to watch is who sits on it. A chief compliance officer, still to be hired. Nvidia is searching for a new chief compliance officer who will report to the board’s Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee. Jones said on Nov. 17 that Huang resigned “after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms.” The person who enforces that code will now answer to directors. Until someone takes the job, it is a promise. An investigation with no verdict yet. A committee of independent directors is examining reporting that Huang “has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” The release says that work continues “to conclusion” and that Huang supports it and will cooperate. Nvidia also said it “will continue to cooperate with ongoing government investigations and inquiries.” Reuters reported on Nov. 20 that Securities and Exchange Commission enforcement staff were examining potential accounting issues at the company, which we covered that day in “Nvidia Stock Just Lost $900 Billion in Its Worst Week Since 2008.” An inquiry is not a finding of wrongdoing. I looked for public companies where a former boss returned while an investigation was still running. Three fit. Each stock move is measured from the last close before the news of the return. Dell. Michael Dell took back the CEO job on Jan. 31, 2007, with an SEC inquiry from 2005 and an audit committee investigation from 2006 both open. The stock closed at $24.22 that day and rose about 4% after hours on the news. Six months later the audit committee concluded that four fiscal years of results “should no longer be relied upon.” Dell spent $260 million on the investigations over two fiscal years. In the last weeks of the fiscal year that ended Feb. 1, 2008, the company was buying back its own shares at an average of $21.39, about 12% below the price on the day he returned. In December 2022 the board told him a return “would not be prudent from a shareholder value perspective” while SEC and federal prosecutors’ investigations were pending. He controlled the vote and put himself back on the board on Jan. 6, 2023. The stock rose 17% that day and stood 40% higher when WWE merged into TKO eight months later, against 18% for the S&P 500 fund (SPY). McMahon resigned from TKO in January 2024, a day after a former employee sued him. The SEC case ended in January 2025, two years after his return, with McMahon paying about $1.7 million. His lawyer said in February 2025 that federal prosecutors had dropped their investigation. UnitedHealth. Stephen Hemsley, CEO from 2006 to 2017, returned on May 13, 2025, the day the company suspended its 2025 forecast. The stock fell 18% that day. The next day The Wall Street Journal reported a Justice Department criminal investigation of the company’s Medicare Advantage business, and in July 2025 UnitedHealth said it was complying with criminal and civil requests from the department. Jones said on Nov. 17 that Huang resigned “after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms.” The person who enforces that code will now answer to directors. Until someone takes the job, it is a promise.

An investigation with no verdict yet. A committee of independent directors is examining reporting that Huang “has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” The release says that work continues “to conclusion” and that Huang supports it and will cooperate. Nvidia also said it “will continue to cooperate with ongoing government investigations and inquiries.” Reuters reported on Nov. 20 that Securities and Exchange Commission enforcement staff were examining potential accounting issues at the company, which we covered that day in “Nvidia Stock Just Lost $900 Billion in Its Worst Week Since 2008.” An inquiry is not a finding of wrongdoing.
So the holder with 1,000 shares owns a company with its founder back and two sets of unanswered questions: the board’s and the government’s.
I looked for public companies where a former boss returned while an investigation was still running. Three fit. Each stock move is measured from the last close before the news of the return.

Dell. Michael Dell took back the CEO job on Jan. 31, 2007, with an SEC inquiry from 2005 and an audit committee investigation from 2006 both open. The stock closed at $24.22 that day and rose about 4% after hours on the news. Six months later the audit committee concluded that four fiscal years of results “should no longer be relied upon.” Dell spent $260 million on the investigations over two fiscal years. In the last weeks of the fiscal year that ended Feb. 1, 2008, the company was buying back its own shares at an average of $21.39, about 12% below the price on the day he returned. The SEC case ended in July 2010, about three and a half years after his return. Dell paid $100 million and Michael Dell paid $4 million, neither admitting nor denying the SEC’s claims, and he kept the job.

WWE. Vince McMahon retired in July 2022 during a board investigation of payments he had made. In December 2022 the board told him a return “would not be prudent from a shareholder value perspective” while SEC and federal prosecutors’ investigations were pending. He controlled the vote and put himself back on the board on Jan. 6, 2023. The stock rose 17% that day and stood 40% higher when WWE merged into TKO eight months later, against 18% for the S&P 500 fund (SPY). McMahon resigned from TKO in January 2024, a day after a former employee sued him. The SEC case ended in January 2025, two years after his return, with McMahon paying about $1.7 million. His lawyer said in February 2025 that federal prosecutors had dropped their investigation.

UnitedHealth. Stephen Hemsley, CEO from 2006 to 2017, returned on May 13, 2025, the day the company suspended its 2025 forecast. The stock fell 18% that day. The next day The Wall Street Journal reported a Justice Department criminal investigation of the company’s Medicare Advantage business, and in July 2025 UnitedHealth said it was complying with criminal and civil requests from the department. The stock hit its low on Aug. 1, 2025, 37% below its level before Hemsley’s return. On Friday, 18 months on, it was still 10% below that level, while the S&P 500 fund gained 18%. I found no announcement that the investigations have ended.

The three cases share one thing. The investigation outlasted the first reaction by a long way: two years at WWE, about three and a half at Dell, and 18 months and counting at UnitedHealth. One of the three stocks was above its starting price at the last reading. Three cases are a small sample, and none of them involved a national security question.

Monday’s jump prices in Huang’s return. The open items come later. Three answers will show how the risk is closing: who the board names to the new committee, who it hires as compliance chief, and whether the investigation’s conclusion is made public.

Those answers will arrive after this story, and The Daily Profit, our free weekday email, will follow each one as it lands, alongside Eric Bleeker’s $1 million AI Investor Portfolio. Get it free here , along with our Top 10 Stocks to Buy Right Now report.

For the retiree with 1,000 shares, the question is size. A position that was worth $125,530 on Friday and about $163,000 early Monday can swing a retirement account by itself. A day when the price is up 30% is a calmer day to decide how much of a retirement account should ride on one company with an investigation still running.

Nvidia has its founder back, and the board has said in writing that its investigation is unfinished, that a new committee will oversee national security and export rules, and that a compliance chief is still to be hired. At Dell, WWE and UnitedHealth, the open investigation ran from 18 months to three and a half years after the boss returned, and one of the three stocks finished above its starting price.
