For those in smaller dwellings, efficient living means maximizing space. That’s where combo appliances like Ninja’s newest microwave / air fryer combo come in. The handy countertop gadget lets you zap your food, then crisp it at the end so your pizza or French fries don’t turn into a soggy mess.

Perhaps no game in history is more anticipated than the latest entry in Rockstar’s sprawling, intricate, and absolutely bonkers open-world series. Grand Theft Auto VI is said to offer a more obsessively dense map, more realism in details like weather and passing time, and more realistic NPCs (non-player characters) than ever before. Here’s hoping those 13 years were worth the wait.

Open-style earbuds aren’t just for the sporty; they’re an entirely different way to listen that keeps you environmentally aware without the plugged-up feeling of traditional buds. The OpenFit Pro take a balanced approach, with seamless open-ear performance and even a touch of noise reduction to dampen the din on crowded commutes.

The old Ironman Timex was a staple for ’80s and ’90s kids, and while you can’t bring back those carefree days, remakes like the Retroware can bring back that carefree feeling. No smarts, no notifications, just a takes-a-licking Timex watch with tactile keys, 50 meters of water resistance, and totally tubular digital graphics.

Serious gamers need a serious controller, and few take gaming more seriously than 8BitDo’s Elite-style Xbox gamepad. From its drift-proof TMR joysticks and motion support to its customizable buttons and remappable bumpers, the Ultimate 3E is the gift for that lovable control freak in your life.

There’s regular Play-Doh for kids, but did you know that Play-Doh makes kits for adults, too? We’re not scoffing. The new Blooms sets take on Lego’s floral bouquets with more realistic-looking flower arrangements, and they include a vase. They’re equal parts nostalgic kitsch and stylish decor.

For on-the-go creators, it’s all about capturing the moment in the highest video quality possible. Insta360’s Luna Pro steadycam offers plenty of features to get the job done right, including 4K vertical video, swift file transfers, four hours of battery life, and a detachable touchscreen that doubles as a remote.

The new Fitbit Air provides the same great fitness tracking we’ve come to expect in a comfortable design that virtually disappears on your wrist. Google’s AI Coach can be overly assertive, but the tracker’s great battery life and metrics for everything from sleep to blood oxygen make it an excellent gift for anyone who needs a healthy hand.

Most mobile controllers have a serious size limit. Not Razer’s Kishi V3 Pro XL, which lets you throw a big ol’ tablet between the handles for a major visual upgrade. It also has high-quality joysticks, great grips, and customizable keys for USB-C tablets, along with haptics for Android models.

So what if you’ve heard “Golden” more times than you can count? Netflix’s massive animated hit is a lot easier to gift now that it’s officially available on 4K Blu-ray disc. The story about three pop stars who band together to save humanity from a demonic boy band is an instant classic, with fantastic music and striking animation.

If you’re contemplating a pricey pair of sleep buds for your loved one, we urge you to halt and consider a softer (and cheaper) alternative. Piercing pillows, designed with pockets for freshly pierced ears, also work great for regular earbuds. Blissbury’s comfy and adjustable Ear Pillow is our favorite. Problem — and sleep issues — solved.

We all do it: pay a ton for a monthly streaming service for just a few series. It’s better to own the real thing, and Hacks , a hilarious drama that follows a comedian (Jean Smart) and her young writer (Hannah Einbinder) in the tumultuous “biz,” is one of HBO’s best series in years.

Hoto’s soldering iron is super cool — and by that we mean hot, as it’s able to reach nearly 400 degrees Fahrenheit in about three seconds. The cordless, adjustable iron makes the perfect gift for your favorite DIYer, especially since it features customizable presets for virtually any job.

For the person on your list whose hatred for smart glasses runs deep, Knockaround’s hip, tech-free sunglasses should hit the spot. They’re available in a variety of fun styles and offer lightweight frames and polarized lenses, with both UVA and UVB shielding for attractive eye protection.

For the coffee or tea lover in your life who’s always headed to the microwave for a heat zap, Ember’s fancy-schmancy smart mug is a luxurious way to keep things toasty. With the ability to set the temperature on the mug or in the app, the Mug 3 makes it simple to keep liquids perfectly hot indefinitely.

Not all reusable water bottles are created equal. Give the gift of a narrow-mouthed bottle, like this 16-ounce Nalgene pick, which makes it easy to take measured sips on the go. Take this advice from someone (me) who bought the wide-mouthed version and regularly spills water all over themself.

If your giftee is into New York City memorabilia or wants a more unique way to light up a room, this cube-shaped lamp, designed around the old MTA entrance beacons, is sure to delight. Locals will recognize the vintage symbol, which still survives in the wild, and everyone will dig the old-school vibe.

Sure. You could put iced tea in them, but no one’s stopping you from sipping pulpy OJ or rich chocolate milk from Kinto’s stylish glassware, which was crafted with an “uninterfering design” in mind. Needless to say, a full set makes a lovely addition to any minimalist’s ensemble.

The hippest thing in audio right now is… the hippest thing from a long time ago. Enter the modded iPod Classic from Player Mods, which refreshes Apple’s media player with some 21st-century upgrades. The 5th-gen model can be customized with several color options (including a transparent case) and up to 2TB of storage.

For those tired of experiencing Joy-Con drift with their Nintendo Switch (or stick drift on any controller), there’s the TT Pro. Loaded with the latest anti-drift tech for joysticks and customizable triggers that let picky gamers have it their way, GuliKit’s customizable wireless controllers work with PlayStation, Nintendo, PC, iOS, and Android devices.

The Pocket Scion is unlike any musical instrument you’ve witnessed before, one that uses the “biofeedback” from plants to trigger built-in synths. The device offers MIDI-out to send digital signals to outboard synths, and it includes an app for both macOS and Windows, finally giving you a way to make your favorite fern a rockstar.

Your favorite gamer needs an awesome monitor, but there are 10 billion options. Alienware’s 34-inch Penta Tandem QD-OLED delivers top-end picture quality, with vibrant colors and perfect blacks, plus a swift 280Hz refresh rate. Best of all, it’s not nearly as expensive as you might think.

Few devices evoke more sheer nostalgic joy than Sony’s OG PlayStation console from ’94. If you know a gamer, Lego’s latest replica brings it all flooding back with several brick-ified details, including a pop-up hinge, a gamepad, and a number of hidden surprises waiting to be discovered.

extraction.body: With Christmas creeping ever closer, Disney has unveiled a selection of gifts for adults that bring together some of the biggest names from its much-loved worlds, including Mickey Mouse, Winnie the Pooh, Marvel and Star Wars. Whether you’re shopping for a Disney fan, a Marvel collector or someone who simply loves a cosy Christmas gift, the Disney Holiday 2026 collection features plenty of options for him and her. From practical travel accessories and slippers to collectible LEGO sets, books and fitness bundles, here are some of the standout Disney gifts to add to your Christmas shopping list. For the Disney fan who is always planning their next getaway, the Mickey Magic 55cm Cabin Luggage Bag combines practical travel design with a classic Mickey Mouse look. Priced at £99, the cabin-sized suitcase comes from American Tourister and is a fun way to bring a little Disney magic to your next trip. For a more relaxed present, the Disney Winnie the Pooh Piglet Inspired Candle makes a cosy addition to any Christmas gift pile. Priced at £19, the candle is available through Amazon . Give the gift of cosy feet this Christmas with the Skinnydip Disney Mickey Bow Slippers , priced at £24 . The playful Mickey-inspired design is ideal for Disney fans looking for something practical while still bringing a little character to their winter wardrobe. Winnie the Pooh fans can also cosy up with the Skinnydip Disney Winnie the Pooh Slippers , also priced at £24 . They’re another easy Christmas gift option for anyone who would rather spend the festive season relaxing at home. Beauty lovers can add some Hundred Acre Wood inspiration to their makeup collection with the Winnie the Pooh Eyeshadow Palette from Mad Beauty . Also launching on 1 September, it’s a charming winter accessory for keeping warm during those colder evenings. For something a little more practical, the Disney Tile Tracker – Mickey & Friends combines Disney characters with everyday tech. Priced at £24.99, the tracker comes from Life360 and is designed to help keep track of important belongings. The books are available from all good book retailers, making them an easy addition to a Star Wars-themed Christmas gift. Fitness fans can channel their inner Hulk with the Myprotein Marvel Bundle – Hulk , priced at £48.49 . The Marvel-themed bundle combines the world of superheroes with Myprotein , making it a potential gift for gym-goers and Marvel fans alike. Prefer Spider-Man to the Hulk? The Myprotein Marvel Bundle – Spider-Man is another option at £48.49 . For the ultimate Star Wars fan, the Mandalorian & Grogu Darts Set offers something a little different. Priced at £299.95 , the set brings characters from The Mandalorian into a full-sized entertainment gift and is available through Amazon. From Winnie the Pooh and Mickey Mouse to Marvel and Star Wars, the Disney Holiday 2026 range offers plenty of options for adult fans, whether you’re looking for something cosy, practical, collectible or a little more extravagant. With prices starting at £14.99 , there are gifts to suit a range of budgets — while some of the larger statement pieces could make particularly memorable presents for dedicated Disney, Marvel and Star Wars fans. For more products from the Disney Holiday 2026 range, shoppers can explore the official Disney image bank and retailer websites linked above.

extraction.body: For a closer look at Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, and the national security implications, Amna Nawaz spoke with Dmitri Alperovitch and James Lewis. Alperovitch co-founded and was chief technology officer of the cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike. Lewis is a former diplomat with extensive intelligence experience. He's now with the Tech Policy Program at the Center for European Policy Analysis. Amna Nawaz: Well, for a closer look now at Huang's return to Nvidia and the national security implications, I'm joined by Dmitri Alperovitch. He's co-founded and was chief technology officer of the cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike. He's now co-founder and chairman of Silverado Policy Accelerator. He's a former diplomat with extensive intelligence experience. He's now with the tech policy program at the Center for European Policy Analysis, another Washington think tank. Amna Nawaz: Dmitri, less than two weeks ago when we spoke after Huang was ousted, you said the board had to act immediately after revelations of his affairs. Dmitri Alperovitch: It is incomprehensible, because, of course, there's still allegations here that are going to be investigated. But, beyond that, this gentleman Jensen Huang has lied to the board. He's lied potentially about other things, in terms of interference with investigation by the Commerce Department into the smuggling activity of the company led by his mistress. And to now reinstate him before the independent investigation is concluded put them in a buy, in case the investigation might return troubling information. Geoff Bennett: Jim, you heard the president Liz's reporting there referred to Huang as a genius. James Lewis: No, it's like Henry Ford and Ford. So nobody wants to say they're irreplaceable, but he was at the center of the AI development program here in the U.S. I'm surprised the board took him back, not because of the bogus national security claims, but because usually when a CEO has an affair with a subordinate, that's the end. So it must have been pretty persuasive, whatever Trump said. Amna Nawaz: Dmitri, we saw how investors have reacted, how the markets have reacted. We know tech leaders were calling for him to be reinstated. Dmitri Alperovitch: I don't think anyone's replaceable. Charles de Gaulle once said that the cemetery is full of irreplaceable people. The reality is that, yes, he's done a lot of great things for the company. You don't need Jensen wan to keep selling those chips. Suddenly, if you are a genius, you can break the law, you can violate corporate policy? James Lewis: I'd say that it's unusual, and I would have waited for the investigation to be completed before I fired him, right? But I do think, if you look at the deals, the financial deals that create AI capabilities that he's at the center of,irreplaceable is a kind of strange word, but he is -- he was central to the casting for the AI movement here in the U.S. Amna Nawaz: Let's talk a little more about some national security concerns that you raised. Dmitri, we heard, as Liz reported, that the Nvidia board said they had assurances of some kind from senior government officials, the president also then saying that he gave them assurances, even as investigations continue to unfold here about exactly what kind of national security risk this does pose. At this point, can we be sure there is no national security risk? Dmitri Alperovitch: I don't think we know much yet. And even just last night there was a New York Times story alleging that Alice Huang, as mistress, had ongoing relationship with the Chinese Ministry of State Security, essentially the Chinese version of CIA. Her husband apparently had longstanding relationships with this as well. If that's the case, and for anyone that knows MSS in China, they would have absolutely used her as a co-optee effectively to tell her to ask questions, to solicit information from Jensen. So we don't know what information he may have passed, either about Nvidia, maybe about U.S. government policy here, whether he was knowingly involved in the smuggling of these chips that she was involved in.

extraction.body: For a closer look at Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, and the national security implications, Amna Nawaz spoke with Dmitri Alperovitch and James Lewis. Alperovitch co-founded and was chief technology officer of the cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike. Lewis is a former diplomat with extensive intelligence experience. He's now with the Tech Policy Program at the Center for European Policy Analysis. Amna Nawaz: Well, for a closer look now at Huang's return to Nvidia and the national security implications, I'm joined by Dmitri Alperovitch. He's co-founded and was chief technology officer of the cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike. He's now co-founder and chairman of Silverado Policy Accelerator. He's a former diplomat with extensive intelligence experience. He's now with the tech policy program at the Center for European Policy Analysis, another Washington think tank. Amna Nawaz: Dmitri, less than two weeks ago when we spoke after Huang was ousted, you said the board had to act immediately after revelations of his affairs. Dmitri Alperovitch: It is incomprehensible, because, of course, there's still allegations here that are going to be investigated. But, beyond that, this gentleman Jensen Huang has lied to the board. He's lied potentially about other things, in terms of interference with investigation by the Commerce Department into the smuggling activity of the company led by his mistress. And to now reinstate him before the independent investigation is concluded put them in a buy, in case the investigation might return troubling information. Geoff Bennett: Jim, you heard the president Liz's reporting there referred to Huang as a genius. James Lewis: No, it's like Henry Ford and Ford. So nobody wants to say they're irreplaceable, but he was at the center of the AI development program here in the U.S. I'm surprised the board took him back, not because of the bogus national security claims, but because usually when a CEO has an affair with a subordinate, that's the end. So it must have been pretty persuasive, whatever Trump said. Amna Nawaz: Dmitri, we saw how investors have reacted, how the markets have reacted. We know tech leaders were calling for him to be reinstated. Dmitri Alperovitch: I don't think anyone's replaceable. Charles de Gaulle once said that the cemetery is full of irreplaceable people. The reality is that, yes, he's done a lot of great things for the company. You don't need Jensen wan to keep selling those chips. Suddenly, if you are a genius, you can break the law, you can violate corporate policy? James Lewis: I'd say that it's unusual, and I would have waited for the investigation to be completed before I fired him, right? But I do think, if you look at the deals, the financial deals that create AI capabilities that he's at the center of,irreplaceable is a kind of strange word, but he is -- he was central to the casting for the AI movement here in the U.S. Amna Nawaz: Let's talk a little more about some national security concerns that you raised. Dmitri, we heard, as Liz reported, that the Nvidia board said they had assurances of some kind from senior government officials, the president also then saying that he gave them assurances, even as investigations continue to unfold here about exactly what kind of national security risk this does pose. At this point, can we be sure there is no national security risk? Dmitri Alperovitch: I don't think we know much yet. And even just last night there was a New York Times story alleging that Alice Huang, as mistress, had ongoing relationship with the Chinese Ministry of State Security, essentially the Chinese version of CIA. Her husband apparently had longstanding relationships with this as well. If that's the case, and for anyone that knows MSS in China, they would have absolutely used her as a co-optee effectively to tell her to ask questions, to solicit information from Jensen. So we don't know what information he may have passed, either about Nvidia, maybe about U.S. government policy here, whether he was knowingly involved in the smuggling of these chips that she was involved in.

sources.title: Amazon agrees to buy Decart’s AI chip software and bring its team aboard - Superpower Daily
passages: Amazon has agreed to acquire Decart’s chip-optimization technology and bring its founders and team to Amazon, without buying the startup or its AI models.
The software is intended to improve performance and costs for Amazon’s Trainium chips across inference and training; Bloomberg reported a roughly $7.5 billion price, which Amazon has not disclosed.
The deal remains subject to closing conditions and regulatory clearance, and Amazon cautions that integration or expected gains may not materialize.
Amazon is buying software and recruiting the people behind it to get more performance from its AI chips.
The intended payoff is faster, cheaper AI computing.
Decart was among the first customers using Trainium3, Amazon’s AI chip.
In December 2025, Amazon said Decart was running real-time video four times faster on Trainium at half the cost of graphics processing units, or GPUs.
Decart’s approach spans software and hardware , optimizing how the two work together.
Amazon expects the purchase to improve its custom chips and inference—the work a model does when responding to a request.
It also expects benefits for training models, including faster processing and lower costs.
The agreement covers proprietary technology and personnel rather than the entire company.
Amazon plans to bring over co-founders Dean Leitersdorf, Orian Leitersdorf and Moshe Shalev, alongside their team of AI researchers and engineers.
Dean Leitersdorf is Decart’s chief executive.
Those include Lucy, which edits live video in real time, and Oasis, which generates interactive virtual worlds.
Decart’s software has also run on Nvidia and Google chips.
Amazon is reportedly in advanced talks to buy AI startup Decart for about $7.5B, according to the FT.
The FT says Decart would help AWS run models efficiently across different kinds of chips, which would mean relying less on Nvidia.
Bloomberg reported Amazon is not acquiring Decart’s Lucy video-editing or Oasis world-generation models.
Globes reported that the deal is tied to performance targets over five years and that the founders have committed to stay at Amazon for that period.
That was an Amazon-supplied result for a specific workload, not a measure of what this transaction will deliver across its services.
Amazon warns that it may not successfully integrate the technology or achieve the anticipated gains.

Eugene Volokh would apply familiar First Amendment rules to AI output while retaining ordinary limits; Alex Tsesis would require stronger human oversight and safeguards; Francesca Procaccini would tailor protection to context and potential harm.

AI does not need rights of its own for its output to raise a free-speech dispute. At a Vanderbilt Law School debate described in a November 23 account, three legal scholars disagreed over whose rights matter —and whether protecting human users should leave lawmakers less room to regulate AI-generated content. The fourth event in Vanderbilt’s Respectfully Dissent series featured Eugene Volokh of Stanford’s Hoover Institution, Alex Tsesis of FSU College of Law, and Vanderbilt’s Francesca Procaccini. Jennifer Shinall, a Vanderbilt professor and associate dean of research, moderated. Their disagreement concerned government regulation of AI speech, not a newly issued court ruling. Volokh argued that restrictions on AI output should face the same First Amendment rules as restrictions on other speech. His reasoning did not depend on treating software as a constitutional rights-holder. Instead, he pointed to companies’ ability to promote messages and users’ rights to create, receive and gather information. “AI output is a joint effort on your part and the AI company’s part, and it should be protected precisely because of that,” he said. His camera analogy made the point concrete: using a manufactured tool to record in public does not erase the relevant speech rights. That position was not an argument against every restriction. Volokh said prohibiting discriminatory AI decisions in sales or employment presents no First Amendment problem, just as prohibiting an employer from discriminating does not. He also pointed to familiar rules covering libel, minors and professional malpractice as tools that could apply to AI. Tsesis argued that large language models lack human consciousness, intention and reasoning, and should not receive speech rights. He wanted legislatures to retain meaningful authority to require human oversight . His proposed federal safeguards included periodic and random platform monitoring, restrictions on data scraping, and protections against autonomous decisions intruding into private matters. Nor did he accept that keeping a person involved resolves the regulatory question. He cited deepfakes, unauthorized real-time facial recognition, social scoring and exploitation of people’s vulnerabilities as risks that remain alongside AI’s civic and commercial benefits. Those were reasons for oversight in his argument, not findings about a particular system. He also rejected audience interest as the deciding factor. People’s desire to receive AI-generated information, he argued, cannot settle the limits of regulation any more than audience interest alone settles questions involving securities rules or antitrust provisions. Procaccini proposed separating First Amendment coverage and protection: recognizing that generated content can raise constitutional concerns without automatically giving it the strongest shield against regulation. She favored protection tailored to context and potential harms, including threats to privacy and autonomy, while preserving the democratic value of sharing ideas. She defended that approach by pointing to different speech rules in schools, government offices and private workplaces. In her account, existing doctrine already adjusts to setting rather than applying one uniform level of protection. She also warned that poorly designed AI regulation could enable censorship or suppression. Volokh countered that her proposal would substantially depart from familiar rules and create confusing restrictions with unknown consequences. Tsesis also challenged it, pointing to existing disclosure requirements and commercial-speech rules that, he argued, would not necessarily fit within the proposed approach. Procaccini’s closing concern reached beyond new AI-specific rules. She warned that courts could use the First Amendment to weaken existing property, civil-rights and tort claims. For her, keeping those ordinary legal remedies available was itself part of the dispute over how strongly AI-generated expression should be protected. His camera analogy made the point concrete: using a manufactured tool to record in public does not erase the relevant speech rights.

Eugene Volokh would apply familiar First Amendment rules to AI output while retaining ordinary limits; Alex Tsesis would require stronger human oversight and safeguards; Francesca Procaccini would tailor protection to context and potential harm.

extraction.body: Vanderbilt Law School’s Respectfully Dissent debate series hosted its fourth debate , titled “Silicon Speech: Should the First Amendment Protect Artificial Intelligence? – A Respectfully Dissent Series Debate.” Three First Amendment experts faced off on whether and to what extent AI speech is constitutionally protected from government regulation. Moderated by Professor and Associate Dean of Research Jennifer Shinall , the debate featured Eugene Volokh of The Hoover Institution at Stanford University, Alex Tsesis of FSU College of Law, and Francesca Procaccini of Vanderbilt Law. The debate kicked off with each professor explaining their initial position on AI speech rights. Volokh argued that government regulations of AI outputs should be subject to the same First Amendment rules as other speech, because users of AI have rights. For example, he noted that rules do not limit the rights of camera manufacturers when people record in public places. “AI output is a joint effort on your part and the AI company’s part, and it should be protected precisely because of that. From your rights as a speaker when you’re trying to generate things that you want to communicate to the public to your rights as a listener and information gatherer,” he said. Tsesis argued that, because large language models (LLMs) lack the consciousness, intentionality, and reasoning of the human mind, AI should preserve the rights of natural speakers and legislatures should have meaningful latitude to require human oversight. “In light of the dangers of new generative AI technology, federal laws should require periodic but consistent and random platform monitoring, restrict data scraping, and establish safeguards against the intrusions that arise from autonomous, machine-made decisions into private matters,” he contended. “In the US, any restriction on AI will likely be subject to stringent First Amendment review in a reductive, formalistic, judicial environment where content restriction is subject to strict scrutiny analysis.” He emphasized that freedom of speech should only be afforded to humans and not to LLMs, which lack empathy, dignity, and individuality. “My suggestion is that you can doctrinally get at the problems [of AI] without sacrificing its potential by drawing on something distinct in First Amendment law: distinguishing between coverage and protection,” Procaccini explained. She advocated for a model whereby First Amendment rights can attach to AI-generated content without having a strict-scrutiny-style level of protection traditionally reserved for people – a different level of protection that focuses on the context-specific harms of AI, from autonomy to privacy, while preserving AI’s democratic-enhancing features. Procaccini argued this position is the best option because it focuses less on the nature of the speaker and more on the nature of the law regulating speech. How does the “human in the loop” of AI content trigger First Amendment protections? Defending his position, Tsesis addressed the question of whether intentional human usage of AI should fall outside of speech restrictions. He established that significant AI progress is achieved independently of human programmers and thus would not fall under the First Amendment. When people are involved in the development process, AI content should still be regulated. “Even when humans are in the loop, the civic and commercial benefits of these technologies go hand in hand with the risk generated by deep fakes, subliminal messaging, real-time unauthorized facial recognition, social scoring, stereotyping, and exploitation of economic and social vulnerabilities such as age, race, sexual orientation, and so on,” Tsesis said. “Ultimately, human audiences’ interest in AI cannot be the final say, just as it cannot be in securities regulations and antitrust provisions.” Procaccini echoed Tsesis’s concern about generative AI running unregulated but also cautioned against overlooking the constitutional and democratic value AI outputs can provide. Procaccini also emphasized concerns about the potential for censorship and suppression if regulations are made without intention. Volokh argued that each concern about AI should be viewed through current laws that perform quite well without restricting speech. He offered an example: AI using discriminatory algorithms for sales or employment. He noted there is no First Amendment problem with telling AI not to discriminate, just as there is not one with telling an employer to do the same. What justifies a lower level of First Amendment protection for AI-generated expression? Posed with how to build a First Amendment doctrine that is not highly subjective or policy-laden, Procaccini emphasized the current complexity of speech restrictions. “Off the bat, I would dispute that characterization of the doctrine to begin with. First Amendment doctrine is not tiered in the traditional way that we think it is,” she said. “It’s very complex… Each speech context is governed by its own very contextual speech doctrine, and most of those free speech doctrines provide some level of intermediate scrutiny. I would say that what I’m doing is nothing different from a very proud and workable tradition of free speech protection, right?” She highlighted how free speech functions differently in schools, government offices, private workplaces, and beyond. Like those spaces, AI-generated content would fall under its own epistemic context. Tsesis also critiqued Procaccini’s approach, noting that AI has a number of other regulations dealing with content, including rules on disclosure requirements and intermediate scrutiny in commercial speech areas, that would not necessarily be covered by a doctrine. If AI-generated content receives full First Amendment protection, whose constitutional rights are actually protected? Volokh addressed how his stance would balance and address harmful AI outputs. He emphasized again that, while AI does not have rights, companies have rights to promote the messages they want, and users have rights to generate the information they want without undue interference by the government. He also agreed with Procaccini on the already complicated nature of First Amendment law, underscoring libel laws, rights of minors, and malpractice regulation for lawyers and doctors that could also apply to AI. “[First Amendment law] already has a lot of rules that allow certain kinds of restrictions. They just have the advantage of familiarity,” Volokh said. “It’s not buying a pig in the poke. We know roughly where they are and the problems with them.” Tsesis circled back again to how AI is a computational model, whereas minds are semantic. Programs are not sufficient enough to be minds and thus should not be controlled by the value of speech. Procaccini cautioned against accepting that traditional legal claims might get at the harms and risks of AI. “Traditional property law, civil rights law, tort law — I have a track record of seeing the Supreme Court manipulate all of those bodies of law when they run up against the First Amendment,” Procaccini explained. “What’s to say that the court won’t take all of these traditional 1L class legal claims and remove them from our toolkit.” She also plainly said that some dangerous speech should be regulated in a checked way. However, uncertainty of those regulations should not be the death to a new and exciting doctrine for the First Amendment. “Respectfully Dissent” presents renowned national scholars on opposing sides of a particular issue. The goal of the series is to highlight cutting-edge perspectives that draw out diverging, fresh viewpoints, areas of contention as well as agreement, and lawyerly argument, while always ensuring respectful dialogue between participants. Procaccini also emphasized concerns about the potential for censorship and suppression if regulations are made without intention.

Posed with how to build a First Amendment doctrine that is not highly subjective or policy-laden, Procaccini emphasized the current complexity of speech restrictions.

“Off the bat, I would dispute that characterization of the doctrine to begin with. First Amendment doctrine is not tiered in the traditional way that we think it is,” she said. “It’s very complex… Each speech context is governed by its own very contextual speech doctrine, and most of those free speech doctrines provide some level of intermediate scrutiny. I would say that what I’m doing is nothing different from a very proud and workable tradition of free speech protection, right?”

She highlighted how free speech functions differently in schools, government offices, private workplaces, and beyond. Like those spaces, AI-generated content would fall under its own epistemic context.

Volokh addressed how his stance would balance and address harmful AI outputs. He emphasized again that, while AI does not have rights, companies have rights to promote the messages they want, and users have rights to generate the information they want without undue interference by the government.

He also agreed with Procaccini on the already complicated nature of First Amendment law, underscoring libel laws, rights of minors, and malpractice regulation for lawyers and doctors that could also apply to AI.

AI does not need rights of its own for its output to raise a free-speech dispute. At a Vanderbilt Law School debate described in a November 23 account, three legal scholars disagreed over whose rights matter —and whether protecting human users should leave lawmakers less room to regulate AI-generated content. The fourth event in Vanderbilt’s Respectfully Dissent series featured Eugene Volokh of Stanford’s Hoover Institution, Alex Tsesis of FSU College of Law, and Vanderbilt’s Francesca Procaccini. Jennifer Shinall, a Vanderbilt professor and associate dean of research, moderated. Their disagreement concerned government regulation of AI speech, not a newly issued court ruling. Volokh argued that restrictions on AI output should face the same First Amendment rules as restrictions on other speech. His reasoning did not depend on treating software as a constitutional rights-holder. Instead, he pointed to companies’ ability to promote messages and users’ rights to create, receive and gather information. “AI output is a joint effort on your part and the AI company’s part, and it should be protected precisely because of that,” he said. His camera analogy made the point concrete: using a manufactured tool to record in public does not erase the relevant speech rights. That position was not an argument against every restriction. Volokh said prohibiting discriminatory AI decisions in sales or employment presents no First Amendment problem, just as prohibiting an employer from discriminating does not. He also pointed to familiar rules covering libel, minors and professional malpractice as tools that could apply to AI. Tsesis argued that large language models lack human consciousness, intention and reasoning, and should not receive speech rights. He wanted legislatures to retain meaningful authority to require human oversight . His proposed federal safeguards included periodic and random platform monitoring, restrictions on data scraping, and protections against autonomous decisions intruding into private matters. Nor did he accept that keeping a person involved resolves the regulatory question. He cited deepfakes, unauthorized real-time facial recognition, social scoring and exploitation of people’s vulnerabilities as risks that remain alongside AI’s civic and commercial benefits. Those were reasons for oversight in his argument, not findings about a particular system. He also rejected audience interest as the deciding factor. People’s desire to receive AI-generated information, he argued, cannot settle the limits of regulation any more than audience interest alone settles questions involving securities rules or antitrust provisions. Procaccini proposed separating First Amendment coverage and protection: recognizing that generated content can raise constitutional concerns without automatically giving it the strongest shield against regulation. She favored protection tailored to context and potential harms, including threats to privacy and autonomy, while preserving the democratic value of sharing ideas. She defended that approach by pointing to different speech rules in schools, government offices and private workplaces. In her account, existing doctrine already adjusts to setting rather than applying one uniform level of protection. She also warned that poorly designed AI regulation could enable censorship or suppression. Volokh countered that her proposal would substantially depart from familiar rules and create confusing restrictions with unknown consequences. Tsesis also challenged it, pointing to existing disclosure requirements and commercial-speech rules that, he argued, would not necessarily fit within the proposed approach. Procaccini’s closing concern reached beyond new AI-specific rules. She warned that courts could use the First Amendment to weaken existing property, civil-rights and tort claims. For her, keeping those ordinary legal remedies available was itself part of the dispute over how strongly AI-generated expression should be protected. extraction.body: Vanderbilt Law School’s Respectfully Dissent debate series hosted its fourth debate , titled “Silicon Speech: Should the First Amendment Protect Artificial Intelligence? – A Respectfully Dissent Series Debate.” Three First Amendment experts faced off on whether and to what extent AI speech is constitutionally protected from government regulation. Moderated by Professor and Associate Dean of Research Jennifer Shinall , the debate featured Eugene Volokh of The Hoover Institution at Stanford University, Alex Tsesis of FSU College of Law, and Francesca Procaccini of Vanderbilt Law. The debate kicked off with each professor explaining their initial position on AI speech rights. Volokh argued that government regulations of AI outputs should be subject to the same First Amendment rules as other speech, because users of AI have rights. For example, he noted that rules do not limit the rights of camera manufacturers when people record in public places. “AI output is a joint effort on your part and the AI company’s part, and it should be protected precisely because of that. From your rights as a speaker when you’re trying to generate things that you want to communicate to the public to your rights as a listener and information gatherer,” he said. Tsesis argued that, because large language models (LLMs) lack the consciousness, intentionality, and reasoning of the human mind, AI should preserve the rights of natural speakers and legislatures should have meaningful latitude to require human oversight. “In light of the dangers of new generative AI technology, federal laws should require periodic but consistent and random platform monitoring, restrict data scraping, and establish safeguards against the intrusions that arise from autonomous, machine-made decisions into private matters,” he contended. “In the US, any restriction on AI will likely be subject to stringent First Amendment review in a reductive, formalistic, judicial environment where content restriction is subject to strict scrutiny analysis.” He emphasized that freedom of speech should only be afforded to humans and not to LLMs, which lack empathy, dignity, and individuality. “My suggestion is that you can doctrinally get at the problems [of AI] without sacrificing its potential by drawing on something distinct in First Amendment law: distinguishing between coverage and protection,” Procaccini explained. She advocated for a model whereby First Amendment rights can attach to AI-generated content without having a strict-scrutiny-style level of protection traditionally reserved for people – a different level of protection that focuses on the context-specific harms of AI, from autonomy to privacy, while preserving AI’s democratic-enhancing features. Procaccini argued this position is the best option because it focuses less on the nature of the speaker and more on the nature of the law regulating speech. How does the “human in the loop” of AI content trigger First Amendment protections? Defending his position, Tsesis addressed the question of whether intentional human usage of AI should fall outside of speech restrictions. He established that significant AI progress is achieved independently of human programmers and thus would not fall under the First Amendment. When people are involved in the development process, AI content should still be regulated. “Even when humans are in the loop, the civic and commercial benefits of these technologies go hand in hand with the risk generated by deep fakes, subliminal messaging, real-time unauthorized facial recognition, social scoring, stereotyping, and exploitation of economic and social vulnerabilities such as age, race, sexual orientation, and so on,” Tsesis said. “Ultimately, human audiences’ interest in AI cannot be the final say, just as it cannot be in securities regulations and antitrust provisions.” Procaccini echoed Tsesis’s concern about generative AI running unregulated but also cautioned against overlooking the constitutional and democratic value AI outputs can provide. Procaccini also emphasized concerns about the potential for censorship and suppression if regulations are made without intention. Volokh argued that each concern about AI should be viewed through current laws that perform quite well without restricting speech. He offered an example: AI using discriminatory algorithms for sales or employment. He noted there is no First Amendment problem with telling AI not to discriminate, just as there is not one with telling an employer to do the same. What justifies a lower level of First Amendment protection for AI-generated expression? Posed with how to build a First Amendment doctrine that is not highly subjective or policy-laden, Procaccini emphasized the current complexity of speech restrictions. “Off the bat, I would dispute that characterization of the doctrine to begin with. First Amendment doctrine is not tiered in the traditional way that we think it is,” she said. “It’s very complex… Each speech context is governed by its own very contextual speech doctrine, and most of those free speech doctrines provide some level of intermediate scrutiny. I would say that what I’m doing is nothing different from a very proud and workable tradition of free speech protection, right?” She highlighted how free speech functions differently in schools, government offices, private workplaces, and beyond. Like those spaces, AI-generated content would fall under its own epistemic context. Tsesis also critiqued Procaccini’s approach, noting that AI has a number of other regulations dealing with content, including rules on disclosure requirements and intermediate scrutiny in commercial speech areas, that would not necessarily be covered by a doctrine. If AI-generated content receives full First Amendment protection, whose constitutional rights are actually protected? Volokh addressed how his stance would balance and address harmful AI outputs. He emphasized again that, while AI does not have rights, companies have rights to promote the messages they want, and users have rights to generate the information they want without undue interference by the government. He also agreed with Procaccini on the already complicated nature of First Amendment law, underscoring libel laws, rights of minors, and malpractice regulation for lawyers and doctors that could also apply to AI. “[First Amendment law] already has a lot of rules that allow certain kinds of restrictions. They just have the advantage of familiarity,” Volokh said. “It’s not buying a pig in the poke. We know roughly where they are and the problems with them.” Tsesis circled back again to how AI is a computational model, whereas minds are semantic. Programs are not sufficient enough to be minds and thus should not be controlled by the value of speech. Procaccini cautioned against accepting that traditional legal claims might get at the harms and risks of AI. “Traditional property law, civil rights law, tort law — I have a track record of seeing the Supreme Court manipulate all of those bodies of law when they run up against the First Amendment,” Procaccini explained. “What’s to say that the court won’t take all of these traditional 1L class legal claims and remove them from our toolkit.” She also plainly said that some dangerous speech should be regulated in a checked way. However, uncertainty of those regulations should not be the death to a new and exciting doctrine for the First Amendment. “Respectfully Dissent” presents renowned national scholars on opposing sides of a particular issue. The goal of the series is to highlight cutting-edge perspectives that draw out diverging, fresh viewpoints, areas of contention as well as agreement, and lawyerly argument, while always ensuring respectful dialogue between participants. Several other factors also set the stage for Huang's return and accelerated discussions with him over the weekend, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations close to Nvidia's board. A sharp stock price drop after his resignation and questions about the leadership of interim CEO Colette Kress also spurred the board's decision, the people said. "I convinced them," Trump told CNBC's Eamon Javers in a phone interview Monday morning , shortly after Nvidia announced Huang's return. "I made the deal," the president said. "It was a lot easier to convince them yesterday than it was a week and a half ago. Trump said Nvidia's board asked for guarantees that Huang, who resigned less than two weeks ago, was not a threat to national security. "And we gave them assurances, at least with everything we know," the president said. "We believe he's fine. He's absolutely fine." Senior Trump administration officials reached out to the board overnight Friday to inform them that Huang had not violated U.S. national security laws, people familiar with the board's actions said. After the White House outreach, the board contacted Huang, who joined meetings on Saturday and Sunday to discuss his potential return, the people said. Huang's spokesman did not respond to a request for comment when asked about his contact with the board and other events leading up to his return. The Nvidia founder resigned on Nov. 12 after reports that he had an affair with an Nvidia employee and with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based company Megaspeed who is suspected of being a spy for China. A report of an affair with a second Nvidia employee broke right after he quit. Nvidia's board named Kress, the company's chief financial officer, as the interim CEO while it searched for a permanent successor. But within days of Kress taking over, some employees and investors who spoke to CNBC questioned her stewardship, as many of them clamored for Huang's return. Kress' performances at an all-hands company meeting on Wednesday and on Nvidia's earnings call with analysts a day earlier were seen by some investors as uninspiring and underwhelming. As the board faced those concerns amid a stock drop of more than 25% over the past week, Huang was aggressively working the phones with major tech CEOs who wanted to see him return to Nvidia, according to sources close to Huang. In the days after he resigned, Huang spoke with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman , OpenAI President Greg Brockman , and Elon Musk , CEO of SpaceX and Tesla , one of the sources said. Huang wanted his job back, but he was not sure what the return path looked like, the sources said. On Nov. 17, less than a week after quitting, Huang issued a public statement saying he was open to returning as CEO. "I've seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO," he said. "NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company," he added. "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO." On the same day, Nvidia's newly appointed board chair, Harvey Jones, told analysts on the company's earnings call that the board did "not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." Kress, the following day, told company employees at the all-hands meeting, "Let's move forward." Nvidia's public stance against Huang returning came as members of Congress moved ahead with plans to interview him at hearings and as criticism grew over the company's business in Asia. The Department of Justice and the Commerce Department, in an unusual joint public statement on Nov. 17, said they were investigating Megaspeed for possible diversion of advanced Nvidia semiconductor chips to China in violation of U.S. export control law. "Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the U.S. economy," the departments said. But days later, senior Trump administration officials contacted Nvidia's board to tell them that Jensen Huang himself was not a risk, according to the sources. The Department of Commerce added Megaspeed to a trade blacklist later Monday. "They did a pretty good investigation, and they felt that he, himself, was exonerated," Trump said . Both Trump and Vice President JD Vance became convinced that Huang was a singular figure who is preventing closed-source model AI companies, such as Anthropic, from getting too powerful, according to a person familiar with the matter, who spoke on condition of anonymity to disclose private discussions. The person said Trump and Vance were briefed on the national security elements of the situation and saw no evidence that Huang did anything illegal or untoward in that regard. Trump believes his administration's close working relationship with Huang gives the U.S. its best opportunity to protect national security and prevent cutting-edge AI chips from reaching banned customers, according to the person. Trump said he spoke with Huang on Sunday, after Nvidia had voted unanimously to reinstate him. "I called him up, and I said: 'I ask you to do one thing, Jensen. Work hard,'" Trump said. "He knows what to do and what not to do," Trump said. "But I just said work hard because if you work hard, there's nobody that can capture what you've done. Nobody, nobody close." — CNBC's Kevin Breuninger and Kif Leswing contributed to this article.

extraction.body: The stunning decision by Nvidia 's board to bring back Jensen Huang as CEO was sealed by a personal promise from President Donald Trump on Sunday that Huang had not broken national security laws, three people familiar with the board's thinking told CNBC. Several other factors also set the stage for Huang's return and accelerated discussions with him over the weekend, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations close to Nvidia's board. A sharp stock price drop after his resignation and questions about the leadership of interim CEO Colette Kress also spurred the board's decision, the people said. "I convinced them," Trump told CNBC's Eamon Javers in a phone interview Monday morning , shortly after Nvidia announced Huang's return. "I made the deal," the president said. "It was a lot easier to convince them yesterday than it was a week and a half ago. Trump said Nvidia's board asked for guarantees that Huang, who resigned less than two weeks ago, was not a threat to national security. "And we gave them assurances, at least with everything we know," the president said. "We believe he's fine. He's absolutely fine." Senior Trump administration officials reached out to the board overnight Friday to inform them that Huang had not violated U.S. national security laws, people familiar with the board's actions said. After the White House outreach, the board contacted Huang, who joined meetings on Saturday and Sunday to discuss his potential return, the people said. Huang's spokesman did not respond to a request for comment when asked about his contact with the board and other events leading up to his return. The Nvidia founder resigned on Nov. 12 after reports that he had an affair with an Nvidia employee and with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based company Megaspeed who is suspected of being a spy for China. A report of an affair with a second Nvidia employee broke right after he quit. Nvidia's board named Kress, the company's chief financial officer, as the interim CEO while it searched for a permanent successor. But within days of Kress taking over, some employees and investors who spoke to CNBC questioned her stewardship, as many of them clamored for Huang's return. Kress' performances at an all-hands company meeting on Wednesday and on Nvidia's earnings call with analysts a day earlier were seen by some investors as uninspiring and underwhelming. As the board faced those concerns amid a stock drop of more than 25% over the past week, Huang was aggressively working the phones with major tech CEOs who wanted to see him return to Nvidia, according to sources close to Huang. In the days after he resigned, Huang spoke with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman , OpenAI President Greg Brockman , and Elon Musk , CEO of SpaceX and Tesla , one of the sources said. Huang wanted his job back, but he was not sure what the return path looked like, the sources said. On Nov. 17, less than a week after quitting, Huang issued a public statement saying he was open to returning as CEO. "I've seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO," he said. "NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company," he added. "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO." On the same day, Nvidia's newly appointed board chair, Harvey Jones, told analysts on the company's earnings call that the board did "not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." Kress, the following day, told company employees at the all-hands meeting, "Let's move forward." Nvidia's public stance against Huang returning came as members of Congress moved ahead with plans to interview him at hearings and as criticism grew over the company's business in Asia. The Department of Justice and the Commerce Department, in an unusual joint public statement on Nov. 17, said they were investigating Megaspeed for possible diversion of advanced Nvidia semiconductor chips to China in violation of U.S. export control law. "Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the U.S. economy," the departments said. But days later, senior Trump administration officials contacted Nvidia's board to tell them that Jensen Huang himself was not a risk, according to the sources. The Department of Commerce added Megaspeed to a trade blacklist later Monday. Trump, during his interview Monday with CNBC, was asked what Attorney General Todd Blanche had told him about potential criminal liability for Huang and the question of whether Nvidia chips had ended up in China in violation of U.S. export laws. "They did a pretty good investigation, and they felt that he, himself, was exonerated," Trump said . Both Trump and Vice President JD Vance became convinced that Huang was a singular figure who is preventing closed-source model AI companies, such as Anthropic, from getting too powerful, according to a person familiar with the matter, who spoke on condition of anonymity to disclose private discussions. The person said Trump and Vance were briefed on the national security elements of the situation and saw no evidence that Huang did anything illegal or untoward in that regard. Trump believes his administration's close working relationship with Huang gives the U.S. its best opportunity to protect national security and prevent cutting-edge AI chips from reaching banned customers, according to the person. Trump said he spoke with Huang on Sunday, after Nvidia had voted unanimously to reinstate him. "I called him up, and I said: 'I ask you to do one thing, Jensen. Work hard,'" Trump said. "He knows what to do and what not to do," Trump said. "But I just said work hard because if you work hard, there's nobody that can capture what you've done. Nobody, nobody close." — CNBC's Kevin Breuninger and Kif Leswing contributed to this article.

The Nvidia founder resigned on Nov. 12 after reports that he had an affair with an Nvidia employee and with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based company Megaspeed who is suspected of being a spy for China. Nvidia's board named Kress, the company's chief financial officer, as the interim CEO while it searched for a permanent successor.

Kress' performances at an all-hands company meeting on Wednesday and on Nvidia's earnings call with analysts a day earlier were seen by some investors as uninspiring and underwhelming.

The Department of Commerce added Megaspeed to a trade blacklist later Monday.

But as tech leaders and venture capitalists rejoiced — “The mistake has been corrected,” billionaire tech leader Elon Musk posted on X — prominent lawmakers in Washington, on both sides of the political aisle, expressed skepticism about Huang's reinstatement and called for more congressional oversight. Newt Gingrich, the former Republican speaker of the House, posted on X that there was something "profoundly wrong" with Huang having a relationship with a Chinese spy and helping China get advanced computer chips. "Congress should really dig into this as a national security issue of enormous proportions and also a significant failure in the federal bureaucracy." Democrats indicated they would not let up on investigating any potential national security risks when they seize control of the House and Senate in January. "The Trump Administration’s rush to reinstate Jensen Huang underscores the need for Congress to act," Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said in a statement. "Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasizing that he’s learned nothing from his resounding election defeat." Schumer said Democrats will "wield their full power" to investigate any wrongdoing by Huang, Nvidia and the Trump administration. "We'll also work on a bipartisan basis to continue advancing policies that stop the flow of our most powerful technology to the Chinese military and other adversaries." Rob Bonta said that the state Department of Justice would continue its investigation into whether confidential information or advanced chips were sent to China as well as whether Nvidia issued statements that misled investors or the public. “It’s wrong, and it’s shocking,” Bonta said of Huang's reinstatement. “And it raises a lot of red flags and questions about tech oligarchy and the president and his involvement, interference, manipulation with this decision and whether, if and how national security is being put at risk.” Huang resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive on Nov. 12, after reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a Singapore-based businesswoman suspected by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese spy. “I can’t wait to get back to work,” Huang said in a statement Monday. “I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution. I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment." Harvey C. Jones, chair of the board, said the board believed Huang is the right person to lead Nvidia. “His reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” Jones said in a statement. "We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company." Nvidia's market value plummeted over the last month, prompting widespread concerns about the durability of the tech sector and the overall U.S. economy. Still, during the company's earnings call last week, interim Chief Executive Colette Kress and members of Nvidia's board stressed that it was unlikely Huang would return: his actions, they said, did not align with the company’s code of conduct. Jacob Bourne, an analyst at Emarketer, called Huang’s reinstatement "a stunning new development, but not an altogether surprising one." "After more than three decades at the helm, Huang has become so central to Nvidia’s identity and the broader AI trade that his departure fueled uncertainty during an already volatile period for the industry," Bourne said in a statement. "His return may help restore investor confidence, but the upheaval echoes Sam Altman’s brief ouster and reinstatement at OpenAI, raising similar questions about corporate governance and the outsized influence of individual leaders over the future of AI." Beyond that, Ramesh Srinivasan, director of the UC Center for Global Digital Cultures, said the episode reflects how central Nvidia has become to the AI economy and thus the economy overall — in part thanks to the federal government’s investments in it — and the Trump administration’s attempt to reassure markets in order to keep backstopping it. “Look at the incredible volatility we’ve seen with the S&P 500 and look in particular at the volatility we’ve seen with the Nvidia stock," Srinivasan said. "I think that this is an attempt to inject some sort of stability in what’s clearly an unstable situation with that stock, and that’s why we’ve seen the short term rebounds.” “Whether we like it or not as consumers, workers, citizens, Nvidia has been set up as just a critical part, a central part of the whole AI game, the whole AI investment, the whole AI economy, and that’s because they are the central chip maker,” he added. According to Angela Zhang, a USC law professor and expert on Chinese tech regulation, Huang’s return and Trump's political intervention provided additional evidence that in “its effort to contain China, America is increasingly beginning to resemble China.” “The market’s enthusiastic response to Trump’s intervention and Jensen Huang’s return may appear to signal a happy outcome in the short term," Zhang wrote on LinkedIn. "But beneath that immediate optimism lies a more troubling question: What does this mean for the long-term integrity of American corporate governance and the rule of law in its financial markets?

extraction.body: Trump says he spoke to the board and that Huang “did nothing wrong.” Nvidia’s board of directors has voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO and chairman of the board, just 11 days after he resigned in the wake of multiple scandals . The reinstatement, announced Monday morning , is “effective immediately” and was based in part on “input from senior levels of the United States government” that assured the board members that “Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” That assurance comes despite Huang’s admitted affair with a woman who, US intelligence sources believe, was working as a Chinese spy and allegations that Nvidia had subverted export controls meant to keep Nvidia chips from reaching China. It also comes despite multiple developing investigations from multiple different government departments into those and other alleged national security, accounting, and corporate governance failures. Huang had been seeking a return to Nvidia since shortly after his resignation, reportedly forming a war room to strategize how best to bring it to pass. Last week, Huang posted on social media that “if the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” President Trump has also been a major backer of Huang’s return to Nvidia. “I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang,” he wrote on Truth Social last week. “It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A.” In a social media post immediately following the reinstatement, Trump called it “the correct and proper decision” and confirmed that “the United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.” Appearing on CNBC Monday morning , Trump said that he had spoken to the Nvidia board “directly and indirectly” about Huang’s reinstatement, and that Huang “did nothing wrong.” Losing “the brainpower of someone like [Huang]” would be “a much bigger threat” than anything related to his alleged interactions with China, Trump said. “We’ve done a very thorough investigation and the investigation showed that… he had bad judgement having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents,” Trump said. “You have to protect our geniuses and there aren’t enough of them.” Huang’s tenure at Nvidia dates back to the company’s founding in 1993, when he and three cofounders were focused on the then-nascent field of GPU hardware aimed at PC gamers. In the decades since, the highly parallel cores in those GPUs have been embraced first by cryptocurrency miners and then AI companies, propelling the company to its position as the most valuable in the world at its October peak. Nvidia stock—the price of which had sunk roughly 25 percent since Huang’s resignation was announced and nearly 50 percent since its peak—was up about 30 percent in early morning trading in the immediate aftermath of Huang’s reinstatement announcement. Huang’s return echoes, in some ways, that of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who was fired almost exactly three years ago after the board said it “no longer has confidence in his ability to continue leading OpenAI.” Two weeks later, Altman was back at the helm after many employees threatened a mass revolt and departure if he wasn’t brought back. In Huang’s case, the revolt following his departure came not from employees but from fellow titans of the tech industry. Executives including Altman, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, xAI’s Elon Musk and Anduril’s Palmer Luckey are among the prominent industry figures who have publicly offered him support in the days since his resignation. In its statement, the Nvidia board reiterated that it has retained independent counsel and formed a committee of independent directors to investigate what it calls Huang’s targeting by “a foreign intelligence effort.” The company has also formed a National Security and Export Control Committee to “oversee trade compliance and national security risks,” and is seeking to hire a new chief compliance officer. This story has been updated to reflect Trump’s statements to CNBC.

extraction.body: Trump says he spoke to the board and that Huang “did nothing wrong.” Nvidia’s board of directors has voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO and chairman of the board, just 11 days after he resigned in the wake of multiple scandals . The reinstatement, announced Monday morning , is “effective immediately” and was based in part on “input from senior levels of the United States government” that assured the board members that “Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” That assurance comes despite Huang’s admitted affair with a woman who, US intelligence sources believe, was working as a Chinese spy and allegations that Nvidia had subverted export controls meant to keep Nvidia chips from reaching China. It also comes despite multiple developing investigations from multiple different government departments into those and other alleged national security, accounting, and corporate governance failures. Huang had been seeking a return to Nvidia since shortly after his resignation, reportedly forming a war room to strategize how best to bring it to pass. Last week, Huang posted on social media that “if the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” President Trump has also been a major backer of Huang’s return to Nvidia. “I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang,” he wrote on Truth Social last week. “It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A.” In a social media post immediately following the reinstatement, Trump called it “the correct and proper decision” and confirmed that “the United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.” Appearing on CNBC Monday morning , Trump said that he had spoken to the Nvidia board “directly and indirectly” about Huang’s reinstatement, and that Huang “did nothing wrong.” Losing “the brainpower of someone like [Huang]” would be “a much bigger threat” than anything related to his alleged interactions with China, Trump said. “We’ve done a very thorough investigation and the investigation showed that… he had bad judgement having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents,” Trump said. “You have to protect our geniuses and there aren’t enough of them.” Huang’s tenure at Nvidia dates back to the company’s founding in 1993, when he and three cofounders were focused on the then-nascent field of GPU hardware aimed at PC gamers. In the decades since, the highly parallel cores in those GPUs have been embraced first by cryptocurrency miners and then AI companies, propelling the company to its position as the most valuable in the world at its October peak. Nvidia stock—the price of which had sunk roughly 25 percent since Huang’s resignation was announced and nearly 50 percent since its peak—was up about 30 percent in early morning trading in the immediate aftermath of Huang’s reinstatement announcement. Huang’s return echoes, in some ways, that of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who was fired almost exactly three years ago after the board said it “no longer has confidence in his ability to continue leading OpenAI.” Two weeks later, Altman was back at the helm after many employees threatened a mass revolt and departure if he wasn’t brought back. In Huang’s case, the revolt following his departure came not from employees but from fellow titans of the tech industry. Executives including Altman, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, xAI’s Elon Musk and Anduril’s Palmer Luckey are among the prominent industry figures who have publicly offered him support in the days since his resignation. In its statement, the Nvidia board reiterated that it has retained independent counsel and formed a committee of independent directors to investigate what it calls Huang’s targeting by “a foreign intelligence effort.” The company has also formed a National Security and Export Control Committee to “oversee trade compliance and national security risks,” and is seeking to hire a new chief compliance officer. This story has been updated to reflect Trump’s statements to CNBC.

The reinstatement, announced Monday morning , is “effective immediately” and was based in part on “input from senior levels of the United States government” that assured the board members that “Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

That assurance comes despite Huang’s admitted affair with a woman who, US intelligence sources believe, was working as a Chinese spy and allegations that Nvidia had subverted export controls meant to keep Nvidia chips from reaching China. It also comes despite multiple developing investigations from multiple different government departments into those and other alleged national security, accounting, and corporate governance failures.

Huang had been seeking a return to Nvidia since shortly after his resignation, reportedly forming a war room to strategize how best to bring it to pass. Last week, Huang posted on social media that “if the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

President Trump has also been a major backer of Huang’s return to Nvidia. “I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang,” he wrote on Truth Social last week. “It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A.” In a social media post immediately following the reinstatement, Trump called it “the correct and proper decision” and confirmed that “the United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.”

Appearing on CNBC Monday morning , Trump said that he had spoken to the Nvidia board “directly and indirectly” about Huang’s reinstatement, and that Huang “did nothing wrong.” Losing “the brainpower of someone like [Huang]” would be “a much bigger threat” than anything related to his alleged interactions with China, Trump said.

“We’ve done a very thorough investigation and the investigation showed that… he had bad judgement having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents,” Trump said. “You have to protect our geniuses and there aren’t enough of them.”

Huang’s tenure at Nvidia dates back to the company’s founding in 1993, when he and three cofounders were focused on the then-nascent field of GPU hardware aimed at PC gamers. In the decades since, the highly parallel cores in those GPUs have been embraced first by cryptocurrency miners and then AI companies, propelling the company to its position as the most valuable in the world at its October peak.

Nvidia stock—the price of which had sunk roughly 25 percent since Huang’s resignation was announced and nearly 50 percent since its peak—was up about 30 percent in early morning trading in the immediate aftermath of Huang’s reinstatement announcement.

Huang’s return echoes, in some ways, that of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who was fired almost exactly three years ago after the board said it “no longer has confidence in his ability to continue leading OpenAI.” Two weeks later, Altman was back at the helm after many employees threatened a mass revolt and departure if he wasn’t brought back.

In Huang’s case, the revolt following his departure came not from employees but from fellow titans of the tech industry. Executives including Altman, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, xAI’s Elon Musk and Anduril’s Palmer Luckey are among the prominent industry figures who have publicly offered him support in the days since his resignation.

In its statement, the Nvidia board reiterated that it has retained independent counsel and formed a committee of independent directors to investigate what it calls Huang’s targeting by “a foreign intelligence effort.” The company has also formed a National Security and Export Control Committee to “oversee trade compliance and national security risks,” and is seeking to hire a new chief compliance officer.
This story has been updated to reflect Trump’s statements to CNBC.

sources.title: Megaspeed, the company at the center of the Jensen Huang scandal, appears headed for a US blacklist
passages: Megaspeed, the company that Alice Huang — the woman at the center of the alleged Chinese espionage scandal involving Nvidia — led for over two years, will be placed on a U.S.
Commerce Department blacklist, Semafor reported Monday.

Megaspeed is a Singapore-based cloud and AI infrastructure provider that, during the period that Nvidia’s boss, Jensen Huang, self-admittedly had an affair with Huang, was one of Nvidia’s biggest chip customers.
Last week, the Commerce Department also announced it had launched a criminal probe into the company.
Functionally, what this will mean is that U.S. companies will not be able to do business with or sell products to Megaspeed without first gaining a special license from the federal government.
Semafor cites anonymous sources familiar with the matter to note the move is designed to stop the company “from obtaining US-made semiconductors.”

This list “contains the names of foreign parties” subject to certain export restrictions designed to ensure that “sensitive technologies do not fall into the hands of those who would threaten U.S. national security or American citizens.” Functionally, what this will mean is that U.S. companies will not be able to do business with or sell products to Megaspeed without first gaining a special license from the federal government. sources.title: Commerce to blacklist Megaspeed, Nvidia customer at center of spy scandal
passages: The Commerce Department is preparing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer at the center of a chip-smuggling controversy, after coming under withering bipartisan criticism for not taking the step months ago.
Blacklisting Megaspeed would bar US companies from selling chips and other technology to the data center and cloud computing company without a government license.
"Treasury, War, USTR and State were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the Entity List for months," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a CNBC interview earlier this month.
The news comes the same day Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive at Trump's urging.
Huang resigned less than two weeks ago amid reports of an affair with a former Megaspeed executive whom US officials suspect of being a Chinese intelligence asset.
