Most mobile controllers have a serious size limit. Not Razer’s Kishi V3 Pro XL, which lets you throw a big ol’ tablet between the handles for a major visual upgrade. It also has high-quality joysticks, great grips, and customizable keys for USB-C tablets, along with haptics for Android models.

So what if you’ve heard “Golden” more times than you can count? Netflix’s massive animated hit is a lot easier to gift now that it’s officially available on 4K Blu-ray disc. The story about three pop stars who band together to save humanity from a demonic boy band is an instant classic, with fantastic music and striking animation.

If you’re contemplating a pricey pair of sleep buds for your loved one, we urge you to halt and consider a softer (and cheaper) alternative. Piercing pillows, designed with pockets for freshly pierced ears, also work great for regular earbuds. Blissbury’s comfy and adjustable Ear Pillow is our favorite. Problem — and sleep issues — solved.

We all do it: pay a ton for a monthly streaming service for just a few series. It’s better to own the real thing, and Hacks , a hilarious drama that follows a comedian (Jean Smart) and her young writer (Hannah Einbinder) in the tumultuous “biz,” is one of HBO’s best series in years.

Hoto’s soldering iron is super cool — and by that we mean hot, as it’s able to reach nearly 400 degrees Fahrenheit in about three seconds. The cordless, adjustable iron makes the perfect gift for your favorite DIYer, especially since it features customizable presets for virtually any job.

For the person on your list whose hatred for smart glasses runs deep, Knockaround’s hip, tech-free sunglasses should hit the spot. They’re available in a variety of fun styles and offer lightweight frames and polarized lenses, with both UVA and UVB shielding for attractive eye protection.

For the coffee or tea lover in your life who’s always headed to the microwave for a heat zap, Ember’s fancy-schmancy smart mug is a luxurious way to keep things toasty. With the ability to set the temperature on the mug or in the app, the Mug 3 makes it simple to keep liquids perfectly hot indefinitely.

Not all reusable water bottles are created equal. Give the gift of a narrow-mouthed bottle, like this 16-ounce Nalgene pick, which makes it easy to take measured sips on the go. Take this advice from someone (me) who bought the wide-mouthed version and regularly spills water all over themself.

If your giftee is into New York City memorabilia or wants a more unique way to light up a room, this cube-shaped lamp, designed around the old MTA entrance beacons, is sure to delight. Locals will recognize the vintage symbol, which still survives in the wild, and everyone will dig the old-school vibe.

Sure. You could put iced tea in them, but no one’s stopping you from sipping pulpy OJ or rich chocolate milk from Kinto’s stylish glassware, which was crafted with an “uninterfering design” in mind. Needless to say, a full set makes a lovely addition to any minimalist’s ensemble.

The hippest thing in audio right now is… the hippest thing from a long time ago. Enter the modded iPod Classic from Player Mods, which refreshes Apple’s media player with some 21st-century upgrades. The 5th-gen model can be customized with several color options (including a transparent case) and up to 2TB of storage.

For those tired of experiencing Joy-Con drift with their Nintendo Switch (or stick drift on any controller), there’s the TT Pro. Loaded with the latest anti-drift tech for joysticks and customizable triggers that let picky gamers have it their way, GuliKit’s customizable wireless controllers work with PlayStation, Nintendo, PC, iOS, and Android devices.

The Pocket Scion is unlike any musical instrument you’ve witnessed before, one that uses the “biofeedback” from plants to trigger built-in synths. The device offers MIDI-out to send digital signals to outboard synths, and it includes an app for both macOS and Windows, finally giving you a way to make your favorite fern a rockstar.

Your favorite gamer needs an awesome monitor, but there are 10 billion options. Alienware’s 34-inch Penta Tandem QD-OLED delivers top-end picture quality, with vibrant colors and perfect blacks, plus a swift 280Hz refresh rate. Best of all, it’s not nearly as expensive as you might think.

Few devices evoke more sheer nostalgic joy than Sony’s OG PlayStation console from ’94. If you know a gamer, Lego’s latest replica brings it all flooding back with several brick-ified details, including a pop-up hinge, a gamepad, and a number of hidden surprises waiting to be discovered.

passages: Whether you’re shopping for a Disney fan, a Marvel collector or someone who simply loves a cosy Christmas gift, the Disney Holiday 2026 collection features plenty of options for him and her.

With Christmas creeping ever closer, Disney has unveiled a selection of gifts for adults that bring together some of the biggest names from its much-loved worlds, including Mickey Mouse, Winnie the Pooh, Marvel and Star Wars.
Give the gift of cosy feet this Christmas with the Skinnydip Disney Mickey Bow Slippers , priced at £24 .

extraction.body: With Christmas creeping ever closer, Disney has unveiled a selection of gifts for adults that bring together some of the biggest names from its much-loved worlds, including Mickey Mouse, Winnie the Pooh, Marvel and Star Wars. Whether you’re shopping for a Disney fan, a Marvel collector or someone who simply loves a cosy Christmas gift, the Disney Holiday 2026 collection features plenty of options for him and her. From practical travel accessories and slippers to collectible LEGO sets, books and fitness bundles, here are some of the standout Disney gifts to add to your Christmas shopping list. For the Disney fan who is always planning their next getaway, the Mickey Magic 55cm Cabin Luggage Bag combines practical travel design with a classic Mickey Mouse look. Priced at £99, the cabin-sized suitcase comes from American Tourister and is a fun way to bring a little Disney magic to your next trip. For a more relaxed present, the Disney Winnie the Pooh Piglet Inspired Candle makes a cosy addition to any Christmas gift pile. Priced at £19, the candle is available through Amazon . Give the gift of cosy feet this Christmas with the Skinnydip Disney Mickey Bow Slippers , priced at £24 . The playful Mickey-inspired design is ideal for Disney fans looking for something practical while still bringing a little character to their winter wardrobe. Winnie the Pooh fans can also cosy up with the Skinnydip Disney Winnie the Pooh Slippers , also priced at £24 . They’re another easy Christmas gift option for anyone who would rather spend the festive season relaxing at home. Beauty lovers can add some Hundred Acre Wood inspiration to their makeup collection with the Winnie the Pooh Eyeshadow Palette from Mad Beauty . Also launching on 1 September, it’s a charming winter accessory for keeping warm during those colder evenings. For something a little more practical, the Disney Tile Tracker – Mickey & Friends combines Disney characters with everyday tech. Priced at £24.99, the tracker comes from Life360 and is designed to help keep track of important belongings. The books are available from all good book retailers, making them an easy addition to a Star Wars-themed Christmas gift. Fitness fans can channel their inner Hulk with the Myprotein Marvel Bundle – Hulk , priced at £48.49 . The Marvel-themed bundle combines the world of superheroes with Myprotein , making it a potential gift for gym-goers and Marvel fans alike. Prefer Spider-Man to the Hulk? The Myprotein Marvel Bundle – Spider-Man is another option at £48.49 . For the ultimate Star Wars fan, the Mandalorian & Grogu Darts Set offers something a little different. Priced at £299.95 , the set brings characters from The Mandalorian into a full-sized entertainment gift and is available through Amazon. From Winnie the Pooh and Mickey Mouse to Marvel and Star Wars, the Disney Holiday 2026 range offers plenty of options for adult fans, whether you’re looking for something cosy, practical, collectible or a little more extravagant. With prices starting at £14.99 , there are gifts to suit a range of budgets — while some of the larger statement pieces could make particularly memorable presents for dedicated Disney, Marvel and Star Wars fans. passages: Amna Nawaz: Well, for a closer look now at Huang's return to Nvidia and the national security implications, I'm joined by Dmitri Alperovitch.

Dmitri, we heard, as Liz reported, that the Nvidia board said they had assurances of some kind from senior government officials, the president also then saying that he gave them assurances, even as investigations continue to unfold here about exactly what kind of national security risk this does pose.
Amna Nawaz: Dmitri, less than two weeks ago when we spoke after Huang was ousted, you said the board had to act immediately after revelations of his affairs.

So we don't know what information he may have passed, either about Nvidia, maybe about U.S. government policy here, whether he was knowingly involved in the smuggling of these chips that she was involved in.
Geoff Bennett: Jim, you heard the president Liz's reporting there referred to Huang as a genius.

And even just last night there was a New York Times story alleging that Alice Huang, as mistress, had ongoing relationship with the Chinese Ministry of State Security, essentially the Chinese version of CIA.

extraction.body: For a closer look at Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, and the national security implications, Amna Nawaz spoke with Dmitri Alperovitch and James Lewis. Alperovitch co-founded and was chief technology officer of the cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike. Lewis is a former diplomat with extensive intelligence experience. He's now with the Tech Policy Program at the Center for European Policy Analysis. Amna Nawaz: Well, for a closer look now at Huang's return to Nvidia and the national security implications, I'm joined by Dmitri Alperovitch. He's co-founded and was chief technology officer of the cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike. He's now co-founder and chairman of Silverado Policy Accelerator. He's a former diplomat with extensive intelligence experience. He's now with the tech policy program at the Center for European Policy Analysis, another Washington think tank. Amna Nawaz: Dmitri, less than two weeks ago when we spoke after Huang was ousted, you said the board had to act immediately after revelations of his affairs. Dmitri Alperovitch: It is incomprehensible, because, of course, there's still allegations here that are going to be investigated. But, beyond that, this gentleman Jensen Huang has lied to the board. He's lied potentially about other things, in terms of interference with investigation by the Commerce Department into the smuggling activity of the company led by his mistress. And to now reinstate him before the independent investigation is concluded put them in a buy, in case the investigation might return troubling information. Geoff Bennett: Jim, you heard the president Liz's reporting there referred to Huang as a genius. James Lewis: No, it's like Henry Ford and Ford. So nobody wants to say they're irreplaceable, but he was at the center of the AI development program here in the U.S. I'm surprised the board took him back, not because of the bogus national security claims, but because usually when a CEO has an affair with a subordinate, that's the end. So it must have been pretty persuasive, whatever Trump said. Amna Nawaz: Dmitri, we saw how investors have reacted, how the markets have reacted. We know tech leaders were calling for him to be reinstated. Dmitri Alperovitch: I don't think anyone's replaceable. Charles de Gaulle once said that the cemetery is full of irreplaceable people. The reality is that, yes, he's done a lot of great things for the company. You don't need Jensen wan to keep selling those chips. Suddenly, if you are a genius, you can break the law, you can violate corporate policy? James Lewis: I'd say that it's unusual, and I would have waited for the investigation to be completed before I fired him, right? But I do think, if you look at the deals, the financial deals that create AI capabilities that he's at the center of,irreplaceable is a kind of strange word, but he is -- he was central to the casting for the AI movement here in the U.S. Amna Nawaz: Let's talk a little more about some national security concerns that you raised. At this point, can we be sure there is no national security risk? Dmitri Alperovitch: I don't think we know much yet. And even just last night there was a New York Times story alleging that Alice Huang, as mistress, had ongoing relationship with the Chinese Ministry of State Security, essentially the Chinese version of CIA. Her husband apparently had longstanding relationships with this as well. If that's the case, and for anyone that knows MSS in China, they would have absolutely used her as a co-optee effectively to tell her to ask questions, to solicit information from Jensen. So we don't know what information he may have passed, either about Nvidia, maybe about U.S. government policy here, whether he was knowingly involved in the smuggling of these chips that she was involved in.

Amna Nawaz: Well, for a closer look now at Huang's return to Nvidia and the national security implications, I'm joined by Dmitri Alperovitch.

Dmitri, we heard, as Liz reported, that the Nvidia board said they had assurances of some kind from senior government officials, the president also then saying that he gave them assurances, even as investigations continue to unfold here about exactly what kind of national security risk this does pose.
Amna Nawaz: Dmitri, less than two weeks ago when we spoke after Huang was ousted, you said the board had to act immediately after revelations of his affairs.

So we don't know what information he may have passed, either about Nvidia, maybe about U.S. government policy here, whether he was knowingly involved in the smuggling of these chips that she was involved in.
Geoff Bennett: Jim, you heard the president Liz's reporting there referred to Huang as a genius.

And even just last night there was a New York Times story alleging that Alice Huang, as mistress, had ongoing relationship with the Chinese Ministry of State Security, essentially the Chinese version of CIA.

extraction.body: For a closer look at Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, and the national security implications, Amna Nawaz spoke with Dmitri Alperovitch and James Lewis. Alperovitch co-founded and was chief technology officer of the cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike. Lewis is a former diplomat with extensive intelligence experience. He's now with the Tech Policy Program at the Center for European Policy Analysis. Amna Nawaz: Well, for a closer look now at Huang's return to Nvidia and the national security implications, I'm joined by Dmitri Alperovitch. He's co-founded and was chief technology officer of the cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike. He's now co-founder and chairman of Silverado Policy Accelerator. He's a former diplomat with extensive intelligence experience. He's now with the tech policy program at the Center for European Policy Analysis, another Washington think tank. Amna Nawaz: Dmitri, less than two weeks ago when we spoke after Huang was ousted, you said the board had to act immediately after revelations of his affairs. Dmitri Alperovitch: It is incomprehensible, because, of course, there's still allegations here that are going to be investigated. But, beyond that, this gentleman Jensen Huang has lied to the board. He's lied potentially about other things, in terms of interference with investigation by the Commerce Department into the smuggling activity of the company led by his mistress. And to now reinstate him before the independent investigation is concluded put them in a buy, in case the investigation might return troubling information. Geoff Bennett: Jim, you heard the president Liz's reporting there referred to Huang as a genius. James Lewis: No, it's like Henry Ford and Ford. So nobody wants to say they're irreplaceable, but he was at the center of the AI development program here in the U.S. I'm surprised the board took him back, not because of the bogus national security claims, but because usually when a CEO has an affair with a subordinate, that's the end. So it must have been pretty persuasive, whatever Trump said. Amna Nawaz: Dmitri, we saw how investors have reacted, how the markets have reacted. We know tech leaders were calling for him to be reinstated. Dmitri Alperovitch: I don't think anyone's replaceable. Charles de Gaulle once said that the cemetery is full of irreplaceable people. The reality is that, yes, he's done a lot of great things for the company. You don't need Jensen wan to keep selling those chips. Suddenly, if you are a genius, you can break the law, you can violate corporate policy? James Lewis: I'd say that it's unusual, and I would have waited for the investigation to be completed before I fired him, right? But I do think, if you look at the deals, the financial deals that create AI capabilities that he's at the center of,irreplaceable is a kind of strange word, but he is -- he was central to the casting for the AI movement here in the U.S. Amna Nawaz: Let's talk a little more about some national security concerns that you raised. Dmitri, we heard, as Liz reported, that the Nvidia board said they had assurances of some kind from senior government officials, the president also then saying that he gave them assurances, even as investigations continue to unfold here about exactly what kind of national security risk this does pose. At this point, can we be sure there is no national security risk? Dmitri Alperovitch: I don't think we know much yet. And even just last night there was a New York Times story alleging that Alice Huang, as mistress, had ongoing relationship with the Chinese Ministry of State Security, essentially the Chinese version of CIA. Her husband apparently had longstanding relationships with this as well. If that's the case, and for anyone that knows MSS in China, they would have absolutely used her as a co-optee effectively to tell her to ask questions, to solicit information from Jensen. So we don't know what information he may have passed, either about Nvidia, maybe about U.S. government policy here, whether he was knowingly involved in the smuggling of these chips that she was involved in.

Those include Lucy, which edits live video in real time, and Oasis, which generates interactive virtual worlds.
The deal runs through Annapurna Labs, Amazon’s chip unit, and Decart’s technology will be used to improve performance on Amazon’s Trainium and Inferentia AI chips, according to Globes .
The Israeli business publication reported that Annapurna co-founder Nafea Bshara led the negotiations for Amazon.

Anthropic was in talks to acquire it for about $6 billion, Bloomberg reported in August , before it walked away in September .
Amazon didn’t say whether that will continue.

Amazon agreed to pay about $7.5 billion for the assets, Bloomberg reported , citing a person familiar with the matter.
“From day one, our mission has been to redefine the boundaries of what AI can do and to make it dramatically more efficient along the way,” Dean Leitersdorf said in Amazon’s announcement.

Amazon confirmed Monday morning that it will acquire Decart’s AI optimization technology, known as the Decart Optimization Stack, and bring on the 3-year-old startup’s founders and team of AI researchers and engineers.

Amazon didn’t disclose financial terms. Amazon agreed to pay about $7.5 billion for the assets, Bloomberg reported , citing a person familiar with the matter. The deal is tied to performance targets over five years, Globes reported .

The deal could boost Amazon’s push to compete with Nvidia, which sells most of the chips used for training and running AI models today. Amazon makes its own AI chips, called Trainium, and has signaled plans to start selling them directly to other companies, beyond its own AWS data centers.
“We believe we’re going to have a very significant business selling chips externally,” CEO Andy Jassy said on the company’s earnings call last month.
Amazon announced the deal the same day Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO , ending a leadership shakeup at the chipmaker that put CFO Colette Kress in the interim role .

Decart’s software is designed to get more performance out of each chip, one of the main selling points Amazon needs to win those external customers. Microsoft is building its own Maia chips , mainly for its own AI services, and Google has its TPUs.
Decart’s software has also run on chips from Nvidia and Google. Amazon didn’t say whether that will continue.

“Every leap forward in AI starts with getting more out of every chip,” said Peter DeSantis, Amazon’s senior vice president of foundational AI models, custom silicon and quantum computing, in the blog post announcing the acquisition .

Decart’s three co-founders are joining Amazon: CEO Dean Leitersdorf, his brother Orian Leitersdorf and Moshe Shalev. Amazon isn’t buying Decart’s AI models, Bloomberg reported . Those include Lucy, which edits live video in real time, and Oasis, which generates interactive virtual worlds.

The deal runs through Annapurna Labs, Amazon’s chip unit, and Decart’s technology will be used to improve performance on Amazon’s Trainium and Inferentia AI chips, according to Globes . The Israeli business publication reported that Annapurna co-founder Nafea Bshara led the negotiations for Amazon.
The founders, who own about 64% of Decart, have committed to stay at Amazon for five years and could receive about $4.8 billion collectively, Globes reported .
Amazon bought Annapurna , also founded in Israel, in 2015 for a reported $350 million. Its engineers went on to design Trainium and Amazon’s other custom chips.

Amazon and Decart have worked together since 2025. Decart was among the first customers on Trainium3, and Amazon said last December that Decart was running real-time video four times faster on Trainium at half the cost of GPUs.

The deal follows Amazon’s release last month of TorchNeuron , a tool that runs common AI code on Trainium with minimal changes. Both moves target the software advantage that has kept developers on Nvidia hardware, as GeekWire explained when the talks surfaced in October.

Decart drew interest from other big buyers before Amazon. Anthropic was in talks to acquire it for about $6 billion, Bloomberg reported in August , before it walked away in September . Nvidia held earlier acquisition talks, according to CTech , and invested in Decart’s $300 million funding round in May.

“From day one, our mission has been to redefine the boundaries of what AI can do and to make it dramatically more efficient along the way,” Dean Leitersdorf said in Amazon’s announcement. “Joining Amazon gives our team the scale, the customers, and the infrastructure to pursue that mission faster than we could on our own.”
The deal is subject to regulatory clearance. Amazon didn’t say what happens to Decart’s AI models or to its existing customers, such as eBay, which is also an investor in the startup.

coreStoryFacts.text: Amazon has agreed to acquire Decart’s chip-optimization technology and bring its founders and team to Amazon, without buying the startup or its AI models.
The software is intended to improve performance and costs for Amazon’s Trainium chips across inference and training; Bloomberg reported a roughly $7.5 billion price, which Amazon has not disclosed.
The deal remains subject to closing conditions and regulatory clearance, and Amazon cautions that integration or expected gains may not materialize.
Amazon is buying software and recruiting the people behind it to get more performance from its AI chips.
The intended payoff is faster, cheaper AI computing.
Decart was among the first customers using Trainium3, Amazon’s AI chip.
In December 2025, Amazon said Decart was running real-time video four times faster on Trainium at half the cost of graphics processing units, or GPUs.
Decart’s approach spans software and hardware , optimizing how the two work together.
Amazon expects the purchase to improve its custom chips and inference—the work a model does when responding to a request.
It also expects benefits for training models, including faster processing and lower costs.
The agreement covers proprietary technology and personnel rather than the entire company.
Amazon plans to bring over co-founders Dean Leitersdorf, Orian Leitersdorf and Moshe Shalev, alongside their team of AI researchers and engineers.
Dean Leitersdorf is Decart’s chief executive.
Those include Lucy, which edits live video in real time, and Oasis, which generates interactive virtual worlds.
Decart’s software has also run on Nvidia and Google chips.
Amazon is reportedly in advanced talks to buy AI startup Decart for about $7.5B, according to the FT.
The FT says Decart would help AWS run models efficiently across different kinds of chips, which would mean relying less on Nvidia.
Bloomberg reported Amazon is not acquiring Decart’s Lucy video-editing or Oasis world-generation models.
Globes reported that the deal is tied to performance targets over five years and that the founders have committed to stay at Amazon for that period.
That was an Amazon-supplied result for a specific workload, not a measure of what this transaction will deliver across its services.
Amazon warns that it may not successfully integrate the technology or achieve the anticipated gains.

Decart’s three co-founders are joining Amazon: CEO Dean Leitersdorf, his brother Orian Leitersdorf and Moshe Shalev.
Those include Lucy, which edits live video in real time, and Oasis, which generates interactive virtual worlds.

Amazon didn’t say whether that will continue.

AI does not need rights of its own for its output to raise a free-speech dispute. At a Vanderbilt Law School debate described in a November 23 account, three legal scholars disagreed over whose rights matter —and whether protecting human users should leave lawmakers less room to regulate AI-generated content. The fourth event in Vanderbilt’s Respectfully Dissent series featured Eugene Volokh of Stanford’s Hoover Institution, Alex Tsesis of FSU College of Law, and Vanderbilt’s Francesca Procaccini. Jennifer Shinall, a Vanderbilt professor and associate dean of research, moderated. Their disagreement concerned government regulation of AI speech, not a newly issued court ruling. Volokh argued that restrictions on AI output should face the same First Amendment rules as restrictions on other speech. His reasoning did not depend on treating software as a constitutional rights-holder. Instead, he pointed to companies’ ability to promote messages and users’ rights to create, receive and gather information. “AI output is a joint effort on your part and the AI company’s part, and it should be protected precisely because of that,” he said. His camera analogy made the point concrete: using a manufactured tool to record in public does not erase the relevant speech rights. That position was not an argument against every restriction. Volokh said prohibiting discriminatory AI decisions in sales or employment presents no First Amendment problem, just as prohibiting an employer from discriminating does not. He also pointed to familiar rules covering libel, minors and professional malpractice as tools that could apply to AI. Tsesis argued that large language models lack human consciousness, intention and reasoning, and should not receive speech rights. He wanted legislatures to retain meaningful authority to require human oversight . His proposed federal safeguards included periodic and random platform monitoring, restrictions on data scraping, and protections against autonomous decisions intruding into private matters. Nor did he accept that keeping a person involved resolves the regulatory question. He cited deepfakes, unauthorized real-time facial recognition, social scoring and exploitation of people’s vulnerabilities as risks that remain alongside AI’s civic and commercial benefits. Those were reasons for oversight in his argument, not findings about a particular system. He also rejected audience interest as the deciding factor. People’s desire to receive AI-generated information, he argued, cannot settle the limits of regulation any more than audience interest alone settles questions involving securities rules or antitrust provisions. Procaccini proposed separating First Amendment coverage and protection: recognizing that generated content can raise constitutional concerns without automatically giving it the strongest shield against regulation. She favored protection tailored to context and potential harms, including threats to privacy and autonomy, while preserving the democratic value of sharing ideas. She defended that approach by pointing to different speech rules in schools, government offices and private workplaces. In her account, existing doctrine already adjusts to setting rather than applying one uniform level of protection. She also warned that poorly designed AI regulation could enable censorship or suppression. Volokh countered that her proposal would substantially depart from familiar rules and create confusing restrictions with unknown consequences. Tsesis also challenged it, pointing to existing disclosure requirements and commercial-speech rules that, he argued, would not necessarily fit within the proposed approach. Procaccini’s closing concern reached beyond new AI-specific rules. She warned that courts could use the First Amendment to weaken existing property, civil-rights and tort claims. For her, keeping those ordinary legal remedies available was itself part of the dispute over how strongly AI-generated expression should be protected. extraction.body: Vanderbilt Law School’s Respectfully Dissent debate series hosted its fourth debate , titled “Silicon Speech: Should the First Amendment Protect Artificial Intelligence? – A Respectfully Dissent Series Debate.” Three First Amendment experts faced off on whether and to what extent AI speech is constitutionally protected from government regulation. Moderated by Professor and Associate Dean of Research Jennifer Shinall , the debate featured Eugene Volokh of The Hoover Institution at Stanford University, Alex Tsesis of FSU College of Law, and Francesca Procaccini of Vanderbilt Law. The debate kicked off with each professor explaining their initial position on AI speech rights. Volokh argued that government regulations of AI outputs should be subject to the same First Amendment rules as other speech, because users of AI have rights. For example, he noted that rules do not limit the rights of camera manufacturers when people record in public places. “AI output is a joint effort on your part and the AI company’s part, and it should be protected precisely because of that. From your rights as a speaker when you’re trying to generate things that you want to communicate to the public to your rights as a listener and information gatherer,” he said. Tsesis argued that, because large language models (LLMs) lack the consciousness, intentionality, and reasoning of the human mind, AI should preserve the rights of natural speakers and legislatures should have meaningful latitude to require human oversight. “In light of the dangers of new generative AI technology, federal laws should require periodic but consistent and random platform monitoring, restrict data scraping, and establish safeguards against the intrusions that arise from autonomous, machine-made decisions into private matters,” he contended. “In the US, any restriction on AI will likely be subject to stringent First Amendment review in a reductive, formalistic, judicial environment where content restriction is subject to strict scrutiny analysis.” He emphasized that freedom of speech should only be afforded to humans and not to LLMs, which lack empathy, dignity, and individuality. “My suggestion is that you can doctrinally get at the problems [of AI] without sacrificing its potential by drawing on something distinct in First Amendment law: distinguishing between coverage and protection,” Procaccini explained. She advocated for a model whereby First Amendment rights can attach to AI-generated content without having a strict-scrutiny-style level of protection traditionally reserved for people – a different level of protection that focuses on the context-specific harms of AI, from autonomy to privacy, while preserving AI’s democratic-enhancing features. Procaccini argued this position is the best option because it focuses less on the nature of the speaker and more on the nature of the law regulating speech. How does the “human in the loop” of AI content trigger First Amendment protections? Defending his position, Tsesis addressed the question of whether intentional human usage of AI should fall outside of speech restrictions. He established that significant AI progress is achieved independently of human programmers and thus would not fall under the First Amendment. When people are involved in the development process, AI content should still be regulated. “Even when humans are in the loop, the civic and commercial benefits of these technologies go hand in hand with the risk generated by deep fakes, subliminal messaging, real-time unauthorized facial recognition, social scoring, stereotyping, and exploitation of economic and social vulnerabilities such as age, race, sexual orientation, and so on,” Tsesis said. “Ultimately, human audiences’ interest in AI cannot be the final say, just as it cannot be in securities regulations and antitrust provisions.” Procaccini echoed Tsesis’s concern about generative AI running unregulated but also cautioned against overlooking the constitutional and democratic value AI outputs can provide. Procaccini also emphasized concerns about the potential for censorship and suppression if regulations are made without intention. Volokh argued that each concern about AI should be viewed through current laws that perform quite well without restricting speech. He offered an example: AI using discriminatory algorithms for sales or employment. He noted there is no First Amendment problem with telling AI not to discriminate, just as there is not one with telling an employer to do the same. What justifies a lower level of First Amendment protection for AI-generated expression? Posed with how to build a First Amendment doctrine that is not highly subjective or policy-laden, Procaccini emphasized the current complexity of speech restrictions. “Off the bat, I would dispute that characterization of the doctrine to begin with. First Amendment doctrine is not tiered in the traditional way that we think it is,” she said. “It’s very complex… Each speech context is governed by its own very contextual speech doctrine, and most of those free speech doctrines provide some level of intermediate scrutiny. I would say that what I’m doing is nothing different from a very proud and workable tradition of free speech protection, right?” She highlighted how free speech functions differently in schools, government offices, private workplaces, and beyond. Like those spaces, AI-generated content would fall under its own epistemic context. Tsesis also critiqued Procaccini’s approach, noting that AI has a number of other regulations dealing with content, including rules on disclosure requirements and intermediate scrutiny in commercial speech areas, that would not necessarily be covered by a doctrine. If AI-generated content receives full First Amendment protection, whose constitutional rights are actually protected? Volokh addressed how his stance would balance and address harmful AI outputs. He emphasized again that, while AI does not have rights, companies have rights to promote the messages they want, and users have rights to generate the information they want without undue interference by the government. He also agreed with Procaccini on the already complicated nature of First Amendment law, underscoring libel laws, rights of minors, and malpractice regulation for lawyers and doctors that could also apply to AI. “[First Amendment law] already has a lot of rules that allow certain kinds of restrictions. They just have the advantage of familiarity,” Volokh said. “It’s not buying a pig in the poke. We know roughly where they are and the problems with them.” Tsesis circled back again to how AI is a computational model, whereas minds are semantic. Programs are not sufficient enough to be minds and thus should not be controlled by the value of speech. Procaccini cautioned against accepting that traditional legal claims might get at the harms and risks of AI. “Traditional property law, civil rights law, tort law — I have a track record of seeing the Supreme Court manipulate all of those bodies of law when they run up against the First Amendment,” Procaccini explained. “What’s to say that the court won’t take all of these traditional 1L class legal claims and remove them from our toolkit.” She also plainly said that some dangerous speech should be regulated in a checked way. However, uncertainty of those regulations should not be the death to a new and exciting doctrine for the First Amendment. “Respectfully Dissent” presents renowned national scholars on opposing sides of a particular issue. The goal of the series is to highlight cutting-edge perspectives that draw out diverging, fresh viewpoints, areas of contention as well as agreement, and lawyerly argument, while always ensuring respectful dialogue between participants. coreStoryFacts.text: AI does not need rights of its own for its output to raise a free-speech dispute.

At a Vanderbilt Law School debate described in a November 23 account, three legal scholars disagreed over whose rights matter —and whether protecting human users should leave lawmakers less room to regulate AI-generated content.
“AI output is a joint effort on your part and the AI company’s part, and it should be protected precisely because of that,” he said.
His camera analogy made the point concrete: using a manufactured tool to record in public does not erase the relevant speech rights.

Eugene Volokh would apply familiar First Amendment rules to AI output while retaining ordinary limits; Alex Tsesis would require stronger human oversight and safeguards; Francesca Procaccini would tailor protection to context and potential harm.
The practical dispute is whether existing speech protections can accommodate AI risks without weakening users’ rights or ordinary legal remedies.
Tsesis argued that large language models lack human consciousness, intention and reasoning, and should not receive speech rights.
Jennifer Shinall, a Vanderbilt professor and associate dean of research, moderated.
Their disagreement concerned government regulation of AI speech, not a newly issued court ruling.
She warned that courts could use the First Amendment to weaken existing property, civil-rights and tort claims.
Volokh said prohibiting discriminatory AI decisions in sales or employment presents no First Amendment problem, just as prohibiting an employer from discriminating does not.

AI does not need rights of its own for its output to raise a free-speech dispute. At a Vanderbilt Law School debate described in a November 23 account, three legal scholars disagreed over whose rights matter —and whether protecting human users should leave lawmakers less room to regulate AI-generated content. The fourth event in Vanderbilt’s Respectfully Dissent series featured Eugene Volokh of Stanford’s Hoover Institution, Alex Tsesis of FSU College of Law, and Vanderbilt’s Francesca Procaccini. Jennifer Shinall, a Vanderbilt professor and associate dean of research, moderated. Their disagreement concerned government regulation of AI speech, not a newly issued court ruling. Volokh argued that restrictions on AI output should face the same First Amendment rules as restrictions on other speech. His reasoning did not depend on treating software as a constitutional rights-holder. Instead, he pointed to companies’ ability to promote messages and users’ rights to create, receive and gather information. “AI output is a joint effort on your part and the AI company’s part, and it should be protected precisely because of that,” he said. His camera analogy made the point concrete: using a manufactured tool to record in public does not erase the relevant speech rights. That position was not an argument against every restriction. Volokh said prohibiting discriminatory AI decisions in sales or employment presents no First Amendment problem, just as prohibiting an employer from discriminating does not. He also pointed to familiar rules covering libel, minors and professional malpractice as tools that could apply to AI. Tsesis argued that large language models lack human consciousness, intention and reasoning, and should not receive speech rights. He wanted legislatures to retain meaningful authority to require human oversight . His proposed federal safeguards included periodic and random platform monitoring, restrictions on data scraping, and protections against autonomous decisions intruding into private matters. Nor did he accept that keeping a person involved resolves the regulatory question. He cited deepfakes, unauthorized real-time facial recognition, social scoring and exploitation of people’s vulnerabilities as risks that remain alongside AI’s civic and commercial benefits. Those were reasons for oversight in his argument, not findings about a particular system. He also rejected audience interest as the deciding factor. People’s desire to receive AI-generated information, he argued, cannot settle the limits of regulation any more than audience interest alone settles questions involving securities rules or antitrust provisions. Procaccini proposed separating First Amendment coverage and protection: recognizing that generated content can raise constitutional concerns without automatically giving it the strongest shield against regulation. She favored protection tailored to context and potential harms, including threats to privacy and autonomy, while preserving the democratic value of sharing ideas. She defended that approach by pointing to different speech rules in schools, government offices and private workplaces. In her account, existing doctrine already adjusts to setting rather than applying one uniform level of protection. She also warned that poorly designed AI regulation could enable censorship or suppression. Volokh countered that her proposal would substantially depart from familiar rules and create confusing restrictions with unknown consequences. Tsesis also challenged it, pointing to existing disclosure requirements and commercial-speech rules that, he argued, would not necessarily fit within the proposed approach. Procaccini’s closing concern reached beyond new AI-specific rules. She warned that courts could use the First Amendment to weaken existing property, civil-rights and tort claims. For her, keeping those ordinary legal remedies available was itself part of the dispute over how strongly AI-generated expression should be protected. The debate kicked off with each professor explaining their initial position on AI speech rights. Volokh argued that government regulations of AI outputs should be subject to the same First Amendment rules as other speech, because users of AI have rights. For example, he noted that rules do not limit the rights of camera manufacturers when people record in public places. “AI output is a joint effort on your part and the AI company’s part, and it should be protected precisely because of that. From your rights as a speaker when you’re trying to generate things that you want to communicate to the public to your rights as a listener and information gatherer,” he said. Tsesis argued that, because large language models (LLMs) lack the consciousness, intentionality, and reasoning of the human mind, AI should preserve the rights of natural speakers and legislatures should have meaningful latitude to require human oversight. “In light of the dangers of new generative AI technology, federal laws should require periodic but consistent and random platform monitoring, restrict data scraping, and establish safeguards against the intrusions that arise from autonomous, machine-made decisions into private matters,” he contended. “In the US, any restriction on AI will likely be subject to stringent First Amendment review in a reductive, formalistic, judicial environment where content restriction is subject to strict scrutiny analysis.” He emphasized that freedom of speech should only be afforded to humans and not to LLMs, which lack empathy, dignity, and individuality. “My suggestion is that you can doctrinally get at the problems [of AI] without sacrificing its potential by drawing on something distinct in First Amendment law: distinguishing between coverage and protection,” Procaccini explained. She advocated for a model whereby First Amendment rights can attach to AI-generated content without having a strict-scrutiny-style level of protection traditionally reserved for people – a different level of protection that focuses on the context-specific harms of AI, from autonomy to privacy, while preserving AI’s democratic-enhancing features. Procaccini argued this position is the best option because it focuses less on the nature of the speaker and more on the nature of the law regulating speech. How does the “human in the loop” of AI content trigger First Amendment protections? Defending his position, Tsesis addressed the question of whether intentional human usage of AI should fall outside of speech restrictions. He established that significant AI progress is achieved independently of human programmers and thus would not fall under the First Amendment. When people are involved in the development process, AI content should still be regulated. “Even when humans are in the loop, the civic and commercial benefits of these technologies go hand in hand with the risk generated by deep fakes, subliminal messaging, real-time unauthorized facial recognition, social scoring, stereotyping, and exploitation of economic and social vulnerabilities such as age, race, sexual orientation, and so on,” Tsesis said. “Ultimately, human audiences’ interest in AI cannot be the final say, just as it cannot be in securities regulations and antitrust provisions.” Procaccini echoed Tsesis’s concern about generative AI running unregulated but also cautioned against overlooking the constitutional and democratic value AI outputs can provide. Procaccini also emphasized concerns about the potential for censorship and suppression if regulations are made without intention. Volokh argued that each concern about AI should be viewed through current laws that perform quite well without restricting speech. He offered an example: AI using discriminatory algorithms for sales or employment. He noted there is no First Amendment problem with telling AI not to discriminate, just as there is not one with telling an employer to do the same. What justifies a lower level of First Amendment protection for AI-generated expression? Posed with how to build a First Amendment doctrine that is not highly subjective or policy-laden, Procaccini emphasized the current complexity of speech restrictions. “Off the bat, I would dispute that characterization of the doctrine to begin with. First Amendment doctrine is not tiered in the traditional way that we think it is,” she said. “It’s very complex… Each speech context is governed by its own very contextual speech doctrine, and most of those free speech doctrines provide some level of intermediate scrutiny. I would say that what I’m doing is nothing different from a very proud and workable tradition of free speech protection, right?” She highlighted how free speech functions differently in schools, government offices, private workplaces, and beyond. Tsesis also critiqued Procaccini’s approach, noting that AI has a number of other regulations dealing with content, including rules on disclosure requirements and intermediate scrutiny in commercial speech areas, that would not necessarily be covered by a doctrine. Programs are not sufficient enough to be minds and thus should not be controlled by the value of speech. However, uncertainty of those regulations should not be the death to a new and exciting doctrine for the First Amendment. “Respectfully Dissent” presents renowned national scholars on opposing sides of a particular issue. The goal of the series is to highlight cutting-edge perspectives that draw out diverging, fresh viewpoints, areas of contention as well as agreement, and lawyerly argument, while always ensuring respectful dialogue between participants. facts.text: AI does not need rights of its own for its output to raise a free-speech dispute.

At a Vanderbilt Law School debate described in a November 23 account, three legal scholars disagreed over whose rights matter —and whether protecting human users should leave lawmakers less room to regulate AI-generated content.
“AI output is a joint effort on your part and the AI company’s part, and it should be protected precisely because of that,” he said.
His camera analogy made the point concrete: using a manufactured tool to record in public does not erase the relevant speech rights.

Eugene Volokh would apply familiar First Amendment rules to AI output while retaining ordinary limits; Alex Tsesis would require stronger human oversight and safeguards; Francesca Procaccini would tailor protection to context and potential harm.
The practical dispute is whether existing speech protections can accommodate AI risks without weakening users’ rights or ordinary legal remedies.
Tsesis argued that large language models lack human consciousness, intention and reasoning, and should not receive speech rights.
Jennifer Shinall, a Vanderbilt professor and associate dean of research, moderated.
Their disagreement concerned government regulation of AI speech, not a newly issued court ruling.
She warned that courts could use the First Amendment to weaken existing property, civil-rights and tort claims.
Volokh said prohibiting discriminatory AI decisions in sales or employment presents no First Amendment problem, just as prohibiting an employer from discriminating does not.
